Here, we combine phosphate oxygen isotopes (δ18O-PO4), nitrate nitrogen and oxygen isotopes (δ15N–NO3 and δ18O–NO3), and nutrient concentrations to investigate nutrient behaviour over a short River Thames, UK reach downstream of a WwTW discharge. The study resolves a high-resolution spatial pattern from a single sampling survey and is framed within a two-dimensional mixing context, in which effluent-influenced water and background river water are transported downstream in parallel rather than as a laterally well-mixed one-dimensional system. Phosphate concentrations and δ18O-PO4 values showed a strong response to the effluent input. Near the outfall, isotope compositions were broadly consistent with conservative mixing between effluent and river phosphate, with first-order estimates suggesting that effluent-derived phosphate contributed approximately 20–55% of the local dissolved inorganic phosphate pool at plume-influenced sampling points. Further downstream, several δ18O-PO4 values were close to the independently calculated temperature-dependent equilibrium composition of approximately 17.2‰, consistent with possible biological isotope resetting of phosphate within the reach. However, because travel times and turnover rates were not directly measured, this convergence is interpreted as evidence for short-reach isotope resetting rather than as a quantified rate of biological turnover. A pronounced low δ18O-PO4 value at approximately 220 m downstream fell outside the range predicted using the measured effluent end member, indicating end-member uncertainty or plume heterogeneity within the wastewater-influenced water mass. In contrast, nitrate concentrations and isotope compositions showed little spatial variation downstream of the discharge. δ15N–NO3 and δ18O–NO3 displayed no coupled downstream enrichment, indicating no detectable isotopic evidence for substantial denitrification over the sampled reach and hydrological conditions. However, the large background nitrate pool means that local nitrogen transformations, including nitrification, assimilation or localised denitrification, may have been difficult to resolve. These contrasting isotope responses show that phosphate was sensitive to both local plume structure and possible biological isotope resetting, whereas nitrate primarily reflected buffering by a large background nitrate pool. More broadly, the results demonstrate that interpretation of river nutrient isotope signals below point-source inputs requires explicit consideration of lateral hydrodynamic structure, end-member uncertainty and nutrient-specific reactivity.

title: Inter-basin groundwater flow pathways and hydrogeochemical evolution regulated by deep fault systems
description: Publication date: October 2026 Source: Applied Geochemistry, Volume 208 Author(s): Xiaoyan Shi, Xingxing Kuang, Meizhuang Zhu, Linfeng Fan, Gexi Zheng, Xinkang Wang, Jianxin Chen, Yinlei Hao, Xiaolang Zhang, Chunmiao Zheng
abstract: Inter-basin groundwater flow (IGF) is defined as groundwater flow across topographic or hydrologic basin boundaries, which plays a critical role in regional water budgets and the global water cycle. On the Tibetan Plateau (TP), IGF has been acknowledged as the primary process responsible for water deficits of drainage basins, with deep fault systems serving as the principal conduits facilitating such flow. This study presents comprehensive hydrogeochemical and multi-isotopic evidence (δ18O, δ2H, 3H, 87Sr/86Sr, and trace elements) to delineate fault-controlled IGF in the southern TP. The results demonstrate that a portion of the leakage water from Nam Co Lake migrates southward as IGF into adjacent river basins along deep, middle, and shallow pathways constrained by the underlying deep fault system. The hydrogeochemical evolution of deep IGF is characterized by inputs from magmatic fluids and extensive interactions with carbonate and silicate minerals, while shallower pathways are primarily controlled by carbonate dissolution and freshwater mixing. These findings underscore the significance of deep faults in regulating IGF transport and evolution. A ternary mixing model of 87Sr/86Sr and δ18O indicates that IGF mixing ratios in local groundwater range from 1.0% to 26.5%, generally decreasing with flow distance. The contribution of IGF to river runoff is estimated to be <6.0% compared with the dominant sources of meteoric water and local groundwater. This study presents a hydrogeochemical framework for identifying IGF patterns beyond water-balance approaches, providing valuable insights into regional water resource assessment and sustainable management on the TP and in other fault-controlled areas.

title: Dissolved oxygen control on manganese release and component-selective DOM transport at the sediment–water interface: A mechanistic geochemical study of lake biwa sediments
description: Publication date: October 2026 Source: Applied Geochemistry, Volume 208 Author(s): Yasuro Fuse, Hitomi Tsuda, Hiroko Okuda, Xue Chu, Yasuhiko T. Yamaguchi, Kazuhide Hayakawa
abstract: Bottom-water deoxygenation is intensifying in many stratified lakes, yet quantitative links between dissolved oxygen (DO) and sediment redox fluxes and dissolved organic matter (DOM) exchange remain uncertain. Here we used long-duration intact-core incubations from Lake Biwa (Japan) under three controlled DO regimes (0, 2.6, and 10 mg L−1 at 7°C) to evaluate how DO modulates Mn/Fe/P mobility and the relative transport/retention of humic-like vs protein-like fluorescent DOM components. Anoxia triggered large Mn release (to ∼40 mg L−1 by day 120), whereas 2.6 and 10 mg L−1 suppressed Mn to ≤0.5 mg L−1 (∼130× lower). In contrast, dissolved Fe and P remained low across treatments (<0.5 and < 0.3 mg L−1). Fluorescence excitation–emission matrices (EEMs) showed preferential accumulation of protein-like signals in pore waters, while fulvic acid–like (FA-like) signals were more evident in overlying waters. Nernst/Gibbs calculations yield a thermodynamic ordering consistent with preferential Mn reduction before Fe under our experimental conditions, though this interpretation remains a working hypothesis pending direct verification. We emphasize that our incubations represent a gas-controlled, closed-water design that excludes bioturbation and advective transport, and that fluorescence classes are operational proxies rather than direct molecular-size measurements. Together, these results provide testable, physicochemically grounded hypotheses for DO-sensitive Mn cycling and DOM partitioning at sediment–water interfaces in stratified lakes.

title: Geochemical controls on arsenic and fluoride mobility in geothermally influenced groundwaters in the Independence Basin, Mexico
description: Publication date: September 2026 Source: Applied Geochemistry, Volume 207 Author(s): Ashley V. Aguilar, Harshad V. Kulkarni, Elizabeth B. Rampe, Yanmei Li, Horacio Hernandez, Viridiana Piña González, Lucía Magali Ramírez González, Alexis Godet, Brian G. Laub, Saugata Datta
abstract: Elevated arsenic (As) and fluoride (F−) concentrations exceeding the World Health Organization (WHO) maximum contaminant level (MCL) (10 μg/L and 1.5 mg/L, respectively) have been historically observed in the groundwater of the Independence Basin (Guanajuato, MX). The co-occurrence of these toxic trace elements has the potential to exacerbate health-related issues such as skin, pulmonary and neurological disorders, diabetes, as well as various cancers. Previous studies have associated mobilization of As and F− with elevated temperatures from a geothermally influenced aquifer subsequently leaching out more of these constituents. This study investigates the role of elevated temperatures in catalyzing the release of As and F− from the lithology which hosts the aquifer groundwater. Geochemical and statistical analyses were employed on 20 groundwater samples collected from the south-central region of the basin to investigate driving factors and reactions responsible for mobilization. Two groundwater sites (n = 2) used for recreational purposes indicated concentrations of both arsenic and fluoride above WHO MCLs. Values of the Cl/Br molar ratio indicated a mixed signature of direct rainwater recharge and organic degradation as important processes within the basin. Geochemical and statistical analyses suggested that temperature can affect groundwater evolution in geothermally impacted regions. There was also evidence of an intermediate mixing zone between source end members. These relationships substantiate previous findings that As and F− release into the groundwater is triggered by geothermal influence because of water table drawdown. The resulting series of geochemical reactions involve silicate hydrolysis and clay cation exchange, leading to As release from iron oxides and dissolution of F-bearing minerals. Understanding the role of temperature in As and F− spatial distribution and mobility is crucial for managing related health risks and groundwater treatment decisions in regions experiencing geothermal influence. Monitoring the intensity of geothermal influence using temperature anomalies is essential to evaluate water quality and should be taken into consideration while developing management strategies for hot springs, particularly those utilized for recreational purposes.

title: Diffusive behaviour of HTO, 36 Cl − , 35 SO 4 2− , and 75 SeO 3 2− through compacted FEBEX bentonite: Temperature-dependent transport
description: Publication date: September 2026 Source: Applied Geochemistry, Volume 207 Author(s): A. Romero-Salido, J. Morejón, T. Missana, U. Alonso, M. García-Gutiérrez
abstract: Compacted bentonite is known for its low permeability and high contaminant retention capacity and considered as engineered barrier in deep geological repositories (DGRs). In compacted clay, diffusion is the dominant solute and radionuclide transport mechanism, making the determination of accurate diffusion coefficients critical for safety assessment. The diffusion behaviour of HTO, 36Cl−, 35SO4 2−, and 75SeO3 2− in compacted bentonite was studied as a function of dry density (1.40 and 1.65 g/cm3) and temperature (25 to 80 °C), addressing the scarcity of experimental diffusion data under variable thermal conditions. Apparent diffusion coefficients (D a ) were determined using two experimental methodologies: In-Diffusion for 75SeO3 2− and 35SO4 2−, and Instantaneous Planar Source for HTO and 36Cl−. Results indicated that D a increased with temperature and decreased with compaction density, following the order: D a (HTO) > D a (Cl−) > D a (SO4 2−) > D a (SeO3 2−). D a values as a function of temperature followed the Arrhenius’ law and the determined activation energies reflects the effective energy barrier for solute transport in the material. For anionic species, D a values were lower than those of HTO due to anion exclusion, more pronounced for divalent (SO4 2−) than monovalent (Cl−) ones. The lower diffusion of selenite relative to sulfate is attributed to its higher surface reactivity, possibly involving sorption through ternary Ca–surface–SeO3 complexes increasing diffusion energy barriers. These results clarify anion transport in compacted bentonite and provide diffusion and activation energy data across temperatures for DGR performance assessment.

title: Elevated arsenic in topsoils developed on an iron-rich sedimentary formation: From multi-scale spatial patterns to human bioaccessibility
description: Publication date: September 2026 Source: Applied Geochemistry, Volume 207 Author(s): Aubry Vandeuren, Benoît Pereira, Tanguy De Ryck, Patrick Bogaert, Johan Yans, Isabelle Bélanger, Pierre Delmelle
abstract: Elevated arsenic (As) contents can occur in topsoil underlain by iron-rich sedimentary rocks, sometimes exceeding regulatory quality standards. This poses environmental and land-management concerns and requires accurate delineation of affected areas. However, the mechanisms controlling the spatial variability of topsoil As content remain poorly understood, often leading to overly and costly sampling strategies that hinder effective management. In this study, we investigate the pedogeological processes controlling the spatial distribution of As and other potentially toxic elements (CrNiPbZn) in topsoils formed from the Aubange Formation, Belgium. Total elemental contents were analyzed across the regional, local and plot scales (0.6, 7.9 and 370 samples ⋅ km−2). Topsoil As contents ranged from 9.7 to 165 mg kg−1, locally exceeding regulatory quality standards. Spatial continuity of AsCrNiPbZn contents was observed at the regional scale but not at the local scale, likely reflecting the effect of long-wave lithospheric uplift and paleoclimatic conditions that promoted lateritic weathering and element reconcentration within Fe oxyhydroxides. At the plot-scale, spatial patterns of AsCrNiPbZn contents are characterized by short-range heterogeneity which we attribute to colluvial redistribution, loess cover variability and differences in parent material weathering intensity. Arsenic enrichment in soil may additionally be influenced by rock porosity during paleoweathering. Incorporation of As into Fe oxyhydroxides reduces As bioaccessibility (from 14% to 3%), suggesting a limited soil–human transfer potential despite high total As contents. Overall, the results highlight the central role of pedogeological processes in controlling natural topsoil As distributions and bioaccessibility, with implications for risk-based soil assessment and management in naturally As-enriched soils.

title: Multi-component soil gas geochemical exploration for deep mineral deposits: A case study from Anhui, Eastern China
description: Publication date: September 2026 Source: Applied Geochemistry, Volume 207 Author(s): Qiuping Qiang, Xin Chen, Yuanjun Xiao, Junaid Khan, Junqiang Peng, Yejun Yang, Song Gao, Jun Zhang, Asma Tahir
abstract: Significant mineral exploration potential exists within the metallogenic belts concealed beneath extensive surface cover in Anhui region, Eastern China. However, mineral exploration in this region is challenged by thick overburden, which limits the effective integration of conventional exploration methods. To address these challenges, a novel, efficient, and cost-effective soil-gas geochemical prospecting approach was evaluated using a Portable Multi-Component Gas Rapid Analyzer (PMGRA) at several representative deposits, including the Hekou Au–Pb, the Jiangshan Au–Pb–Zn, the Zhongjiashan Pb–Zn (Au–Ag), and the Dongsunjia Cu deposits. Soil-gas measurements indicate that the enrichment coefficients of H2S (0.9-9.4) and SO2 (0.8-7.4), together with the newly introduced gases H2 (1.0-22.8) and CS2 (0.5-17.9), are consistently elevated above concealed sulfide mineralization. Their spatial distributions are strongly controlled by orebody geometry. CO2 anomalies predominantly reflect subsurface fault systems, and the spatial coincidence of CO2 anomalies with H2 and sulfur-bearing gas anomalies represents a reliable criterion for identifying ore-bearing structures. Certain segments within the non-mineralized zones of the exploration-line profiles across the Hekou Au–Pb, Jiangshan Au–Pb–Zn, and Zhongjiashan Pb–Zn (Au–Ag) deposits exhibit pronounced anomalies of H2S, SO2, CS2, and H2. These observations indicate that the exploration area retains substantial prospecting potential and suggest the possible presence of additional concealed ore bodies or previously unrecognized mineralized zones. Further detailed investigations are therefore required to verify and delineate these prospective targets. H2S, SO2, CS2, and H2 are the most effective and sensitive pathfinders for the Dongsunjia Cu deposit compared to the other Au–Pb–Zn–Ag deposits. Overall, soil-gas analysis of H2S, SO2, H2, CS2, and CO2 using PMGRA is effective for detecting deep-buried sulfide orebodies in covered terrains and provides a practical approach for mineral exploration.

title: Molecular and macroscopic insights into hydrocarbon contamination removal from minerals using maple-derived saponin with focus on hydrocarbon chemistry and mineral type
description: Publication date: September 2026 Source: Applied Geochemistry, Volume 207 Author(s): Arezoo Rezaei, Saeed Karami, Mohsen Rahmati, Fatemeh Khajouei, Azam Motaghi
abstract: This study introduces a novel saponin derived from municipally-collected maple leaves for effective hydrocarbon contaminant separation from polluted minerals that are common soil components. To gain in-depth mechanistic insight, four hydrocarbons of crude oil, asphaltene, stearic acid, and paraffin, were used to simulate the removal of various contaminants from pure silica (quartz) and calcium carbonate (calcite) minerals. The contaminating hydrocarbons were characterized using FTIR and NMR spectroscopy to elucidate their chemical composition and molecular structure. 1H NMR and FTIR analyses revealed that the maple-derived saponin is predominantly composed of glycosides and carbohydrates. To investigate both the macroscopic and molecular mechanisms of contaminant removal, static removal tests, hydrocarbon solubility measurements, FTIR analysis, saponin adsorption studies, and contact angle measurements were performed. The maple-derived saponin demonstrated substantial efficacy, removing 71-88% of hydrocarbons within 24 h at 25 °C during static separation tests. Hydrocarbon removal was higher from silica than from calcium carbonate, indicating stronger intermolecular attractions with the latter. FTIR analysis revealed selective trends in contaminating compound desorption, with asphaltenes from calcium carbonate showing higher polarity, higher aromaticity, and longer aliphatic chains. Contact angle measurements showed the saponin's effectiveness in improving the substrate hydrophilicity across mineral and hydrocarbon types. The highest wettability improvement was observed in stearic acid-contaminated silica (109.92%), and the lowest was in paraffin-contaminated silica (24.87%). This study demonstrates the viability of a cost-effective, maple-derived saponin for removing petroleum contaminants from diverse mineral substrates, holding promise for soil preservation, particularly in cold climates where maple forests are abundant.

title: Deep degassing in the southeastern margin of the Tibetan Plateau: Fluid fluxes, sources, and tectonic implications of the Ganzi-Litang suture zone
description: Publication date: September 2026 Source: Applied Geochemistry, Volume 207 Author(s): Deyang Zhao, Xiaocheng Zhou, Miao He, Jiao Tian, Yao Yang, Ju Zhang, Jingchao Li, Jinyuan Dong, Yucong Yan, Zhaojun Zeng, Yuwen Wang
abstract: The Ganzi-Litang suture zone (GLSZ), a key tectonic boundary in the southeastern Tibetan Plateau, plays a crucial role in understanding plateau uplift and evolution through its deep cycling processes. This study presents a systematic geochemical investigation of gases from 17 hot springs along this suture zone, analyzing He and CO2 concentrations and isotopic compositions (3He/4He, δ13C–CO2) to elucidate deep fluid sources, migration mechanisms, and their tectonic connections. Results show that the 3He/4He ratios (Rc/Ra) of spring gases range from 0.08 to 0.91, indicating a predominance of crustal radiogenic helium with a minor (1–11%Ra) but significant mantle-derived component, confirming the fault system as an effective conduit for upward migration of mantle volatiles. CO2 is primarily sourced from metamorphic decarbonation of crustal carbonate rocks and thermal decomposition of organic sediments (combined contribution >98%). The large variation in CO2/3He ratios (107–1012), negatively correlated with He concentration, reveals preferential degassing of He and subsequent CO2 consumption via calcite precipitation during hydrothermal ascent. A one-dimensional model reveals a high mantle-derived fluid ascent rate of up to 782.9 mm/y. The 3He flux (103–104 atoms m−2 s−1) is significantly higher than that of stable continental blocks, indicating active deep degassing. Temporal variations in gas composition correlate with seismic events, and spatial correlation exists between high 3He/4He anomalies and deep crustal low-velocity zones. This study reveals profound crust-mantle interaction within the GLSZ, highlighting its role as a key pathway for deep volatile migration, and provides crucial geochemical constraints on the tectonic evolution and crustal dynamics of the southeastern Tibetan Plateau.

title: Effects of secondary hydrothermal fluids on gallium distribution and coordination in hot springs silica using Ga K-edge XANES
description: Publication date: September 2026 Source: Applied Geochemistry, Volume 207 Author(s): M.C. Rowe, K.A. Campbell, D.A. Stallard, B. Lyon, A. Langendam, E. Kalinina, M. Yamanaka, R. Tanaka, T. Christopher, S.W. Ruff, E. Nersezova, T. Ota, A. Hamilton
abstract: Gallium (Ga), a critical element in the electronics industry, is enriched in hot spring silica deposits (sinter) at concentrations comparable to, and in some cases greater than, bauxite, coal, and sphalerite deposits from which it is currently extracted. Focusing on well characterized Holocene and Pleistocene New Zealand sinters, we utilize synchrotron-X-ray fluorescence (sXRF) and Ga K-edge X-ray absorption near edge structure (XANES) spectroscopy to examine the spatial distribution of Ga as well as its changing coordination number. Ga+3 is the only observed oxidation state in the analyzed sinters. Gallium is predominantly found in tetrahedral coordination in sinter deposited from alkali chloride fluids, with analyses best matching Ga-aluminosilicate standards. However, Ga coordination is octahedral in sinter samples that have undergone alteration by acidic fluids/gases, associated with a change in hydrology from alkali-chloride to acid-sulfate fluid conditions. High Ga concentrations are found associated with both these coordination environments, with a heterogeneous distribution. Octahedral Ga is observed both as particles and in larger regions affected by Fe-rich fluid overprinting. The combined use of sXRF and XANES demonstrates an ability to fingerprint diagenesis and alteration in these complex geothermal settings where tetrahedral and octahedral Ga co-exist. The transition from tetrahedral to octahedral Ga also appears to mimic the inferred natural process forming lateritic bauxite deposits, where remobilized tetrahedral Ga is reconcentrated and adsorbed to oxides. A similar process may occur for sinter Ga enrichment, whereby introduced Ga in acidic conditions is adsorbed to oxide phases as the Fe-rich secondary fluids infiltrate porous sinter material.

title: Dissolution kinetics of platinum mine by-products for nature-based and engineered carbon dioxide removal
description: Publication date: September 2026 Source: Applied Geochemistry, Volume 207 Author(s): L.A. Bullock, A. Cunningham, J. Matter, D. Hasson, E. Smith, M.T. Duret, E.M. Mervine, R.H. James, D.A.H. Teagle
abstract: In addition to deep reductions in greenhouse gas emissions, active removal of atmospheric CO2 is essential to limit global warming to <2 °C above pre-industrial levels. Dissolution of crushed silicate rocks by carbonic acid converts CO2 into stable carbon species (alkalinity, carbonate minerals), but its effectiveness for CO2 removal (CDR) depends on identifying suitably abundant and reactive feedstocks. Here, we assess dissolution rates of crushed by-products (overburden, processed tailings, smelter slags) from platinum group metal (PGM) mining operations within the Bushveld Complex, South Africa, during reaction with water and CO2 under far from equilibrium conditions. Mine tailings had fastest bulk dissolution rates (∼10−10 to 10−8 mol m−2 s−1), with fresh material sourced directly from concentrator conveyor belts reacting faster than tailings collected from settling ponds. Glassy slag material dissolved at rates of 10−11 to 10−9 mol m−2 s−1, whereas plagioclase-rich overburden rocks reacted more slowly, with dissolution rates of 10−12 to 10−10 mol m−2 s−1. Finer-grained overburden material generally dissolved more slowly than coarser fractions, likely due to particle clustering, surface passivation and/or enrichment of slower-reacting clays in finer material. Under CO2-saturated conditions, relative bulk dissolution rates of PGM by-products were generally faster (by ∼1-3 orders of magnitude) than for other potential CDR feedstocks, such as basalt and gabbro. At the global scale, weathering of PGM by-products has the potential to sequester up to one gigatonne of CO2 per year, of which the Bushveld Complex may account for as much as 75%. However, we caution that while our experiments show that PGM by-products have high intrinsic reactivity, they are unlikely to deliver durable and substantial CDR under field conditions where factors such as availability of CO2 and soil water flow rate may inhibit dissolution. The CDR potential of PGM by-products is only likely to be fully realised with process intensification, such as using reactors or through microbial augmentation.

title: Geochemical divergence of oxygen and sulfur compounds in high-maturity bitumen: Implications for thermal maturity assessment
description: Publication date: September 2026 Source: Applied Geochemistry, Volume 207 Author(s): Chi Zhang, Quanyou Liu, Huiyuan Xu, Pengpeng Li, Dongya Zhu, Biqing Zhu
abstract: Bitumen contains abundant nitrogen-, sulfur-, and oxygen-bearing (NSO) compounds whose molecular structures record critical geological information. To enhance the evaluation of high-to over-mature stages rock or sediment samples, due to the highly thermal destruction of molecular biomarkers, this study analyzes high-maturity bitumen from the Tarim Basin, China. The molecular geochemical results reveal that the evolution of organic matter at high-maturity stages is dominated by thermal cracking, ring-opening, and hydrogenation reactions. This process leads to a reversal in the molecular distribution trends of oxygen-containing compounds compared to those observed at low-to medium-maturity stages: complex “precursor” molecules with high double bond equivalents (DBE) and high carbon numbers are consumed, while simpler “product” molecules with low DBE and low carbon numbers become relatively enriched. In contrast, aromatic sulfur compounds (S1class) exhibit no significant differences in their DBE distribution patterns across samples of varying maturity due to their higher thermal stability. This suggests that they may exist in a “dynamic equilibrium” between condensation and cracking, which diminishes their utility as maturity indicators. Based on these systematic evolutionary patterns, this study proposed a series of novel maturity parameters i.e., the DBE1-5O2/DBE8-15O2 and C6-23DBE0-21O/C24-45DBE0-21O ratios. These novel parameters demonstrate excellent linear correlations with aromatic maturity parameters based on alkylphenanthrene, alkylnaphthalene, etc., whose effectiveness has been extensively validated, and can serve as effective complementary tools for the evaluation of high-to over-mature source rocks and crude oils, providing new molecular geochemical approaches for deep hydrocarbon exploration.

title: Meromictic stratification and geochemical gradients in a flooded abandoned apatite and mica mine (Quebec, Canada)
description: Publication date: September 2026 Source: Applied Geochemistry, Volume 207 Author(s): Élisa Pastier, Élise Lhoste, David Jaclin, Cassandre Sara Lazar, Violaine Ponsin
abstract: Mining resources are important in Canada, which has led to many abandoned mines prior to the 1991 mining regulations. Flooded mines that do not pose immediate risks to the environment or human health remain understudied. This study investigates the hydrochemistry and density stratification of a flooded apatite and mica mine (an open pit lake connected to underground levels) in Quebec, focusing on depth-dependent gradients and seasonal variations. Vertical profiling revealed a meromictic structure consisting of three layers: an oxic mixolimnion extending to a depth of 8 – 9 m, a transition zone characterized by a thermocline and chemocline, and a permanently anoxic monimolimnion below 11 m. Seasonal variations were confined to the mixolimnion, whereas deeper water remained chemically and physically stable throughout the sampling period, from early May to the end of October. Stable water isotope data further support the stratification, with shallow samples showing evaporation, deep samples aligning with the Local Meteoric Water Line (LMWL), and very few intermediate data points. The open-pit morphometry, the steep slopes surrounding the lake, and density differences were very likely responsible for the development of meromixis. δ34S–SO4 values indicate active microbial sulfate reduction in the chemocline and the anoxic monimolimnion, while the precipitation of carbonates and metal sulfides control the chemistry of the monimolimnion. Phosphorus and nitrogen accumulated in the mixolimnion following the establishment of stable water column stratification. These findings identify the Blackburn Mine as a valuable model for investigating hydrochemical and biogeochemical processes in flooded mica and apatite mines, and for improving our understanding of density and thermal stratification in subsurface aquatic environments.

title: A high-fraction of O 2 incorporation in sulfate derived from hydrogen sulfide oxidation at pH of 8
description: Publication date: September 2026 Source: Applied Geochemistry, Volume 207 Author(s): Fumihiro Matsu'ura, Xiaobin Cao, Shohei Hattori, Zhao Wei, Zhenfei Wang, Huiming Bao
abstract: Oxidation of hydrogen sulfide to sulfate is commonly occurring at the redoxcline of oceans and freshwater systems, producing newly formed sulfate with δ18O and δ34S values different from those of the original sulfate. Hydrogen sulfide oxidation leads to the formation of several sulfur oxide species, occurs with various oxidants such as O2 and Fe3+, and proceeds through both biotic and abiotic pathways. A large number of biotic and abiotic sulfide oxidation experiments have been conducted to elucidate the complex pathway using oxygen isotopes. Oxygen atoms in sulfate are derived from both O2 and H2O during sulfide oxidation, which allows us to disentangle the oxidants involved in the reaction and further clarify the detailed mechanism. However, the oxygen isotope behaviors during hydrogen sulfide oxidation, particularly the fractions of oxygen from H2O or O2 being incorporated into sulfate, are inconsistent in literature. Besides, many of the sulfide oxidation experiments have been conducted in low pH condition (around 2), targeting the sulfur cycle in extreme environment such as acid-mine drainages. The low pH condition enhances oxygen exchange with sulfite and water, possibly reducing the fraction of O2-derived oxygen in the product sulfate. To address this issue, we conducted both biotic (using Cupriavidus pinatubonensis JMP134) and abiotic HS− oxidation experiments at pH 8 with 17O-labeled water to quantify the proportion of dissolved O2 in the resulting sulfate. The oxygen isotope analyses revealed that 88.6 ± 1.1% of the oxygen in product sulfate was derived from dissolved O2 during aerobic abiotic HS− oxidation. This fraction exceeds both the 67% concluded in a previous 18O-labeled experimental study and the less than 75% predicted by the abiotic HS− oxidation model, indicating the dominant portion of the sulfate must have been formed via a pathway that bypasses the intermediate sulfite or bisulfite. In addition, we determined the apparent kinetic isotope effect (AKIE) during O2 incorporation into sulfate at 18εSO4−O2 = −12.2 ± 0.7‰. These results suggest that a large O2 fraction could be incorporated into product sulfate during HS− oxidation at close-to-modern seawater pH condition.

title: Migration and transformation of antimony during Fe(II)-induced ferrihydrite recrystallization under anaerobic conditions
description: Publication date: September 2026 Source: Applied Geochemistry, Volume 207 Author(s): Chengjun Zhang, Mengchang He, Huiji Liu, Matthew I. Leybourne, Tangfu Xiao
abstract: Ferrihydrite can transform into more stable iron oxide minerals, including goethite and lepidocrocite, in the presence of dissolved Fe(II) under anaerobic conditions. During these recrystallization processes, variations in the adsorption capacity of iron oxide minerals, potential crystalline incorporation, and electron transfer processes may influence the fate of coexisting antimony. In the present study, antimony migration and transformation during the Fe(II)-induced recrystallization of ferrihydrite were systematically investigated under anaerobic conditions with different antimony speciation and concentrations. The results revealed that about 42–61% of the total antimony was eventually sequestered in the solid phase in a more stable form than simple surface adsorption occurred, and about 62–80% of the initial Sb(III) was oxidized to Sb(V) in systems containing Sb(III). X-ray diffraction (XRD), X-ray photoelectron spectroscopy (XPS), Fourier transform infrared (FT-IR) results indicated that the presence of both Sb(V) and Sb(III) promoted the Fe(II)-induced recrystallization of ferrihydrite, and this effect gradually weakened with increasing antimony concentration. The influence of Sb(III) was more pronounced. Under conditions with Fe:Sb molar ratios of 100 and 80, goethite was the dominant transformation product, whereas lepidocrocite became the main product at an Fe:Sb molar ratio of 40. These results suggest that Fe(II)-induced recrystallization of ferrihydrite may help reduce the mobility and toxicity of Sb in anoxic aquifers.

title: Assessing groundwater-surface water interactions in an anthropized alluvial aquifer by combining hydrochemical and isotopic data with a statistical approach
description: Publication date: September 2026 Source: Applied Geochemistry, Volume 207 Author(s): H. Mahamat, A.L. Cognard-Plancq, E. Gibert, C. Lynde, N. Barthelemy, G. Daniel, S. Savoye
abstract: To better understand the dynamics of groundwater in an anthropized alluvial aquifer in the Lower Rhône Valley, we applied multivariate statistical methods including hierarchical clustering analysis (HCA) to two datasets. The first dataset included conservative tracers (Cl−, Br− and stable water isotopes, δ2H and δ18O) and comprised 667 water samples. The second dataset included major and minor ions (Ca2+, Mg2+, K+, Na+, Cl−, SO4 2, alkalinity, NO3−, Br− and U(VI)) and stable water isotopes (δ2H and δ18O), comprising 374 water samples. Cluster analysis and dimension reduction techniques applied to the conservative tracer dataset revealed three groups of groundwater distributed between two recharge sources, as shown by the resulting distribution maps of clusters and boxplots. 1) The first group was characterized by Rhône recharge and was located along the Rhône River boundary. This group was characterized by highly depleted δ2H (mean = - 66.7‰) and δ18O (mean = −9.5‰) signatures. 2) Rainfall Recharge: Groundwater located along the northern and northwestern parts of the site. This group was characterized by highly enriched δ2H (mean = −41.4‰) and δ18O (mean = −6.4‰) signatures. 3) The third group, Mixing Recharge, was predominantly distributed in the southern part of the site and was characterized by intermediate δ2H and δ18O signatures. Additionally, the HCA analysis revealed the influence of 2022 Saharan dust event on the signatures of rainwater, the Rhône River, and thus, groundwater, with high deuterium excess, calcium and chloride concentrations. Cluster analysis of the second dataset identified water samples with high uranium and chloride concentrations, consistent with historical pollution in the area. Conversely, the results revealed temporal variations in groundwater and surface water linked to rainfalls events. Changes in the HCA cluster index and chloride concentrations suggest vertical infiltration or lateral inflow. This approach provides a better understanding of local-scale groundwater dynamics in an anthropized alluvial aquifer and offers valuable insights for groundwater management and modeling.

title: Can mine tailings be recycled in soil ecosystems? A mineralogical and chemical examination of their suitability for recycling
description: Publication date: September 2026 Source: Applied Geochemistry, Volume 207 Author(s): Olga Odrzygóźdź, Nikita Malafeevskiy, Trine Aulstad Sogn, Stefanie Lode, Kurt Aasly
abstract: Mine tailings represent a valuable secondary resource with strong potential for material recovery. This study presents a detailed mineralogical and chemical characterization of mineral materials from three Norwegian deposits - mine tailings from Rana iron formation (R tailings), and lab-scale tailings from mineral processing of the Fen carbonatite complex (C tailings) and Nussir copper deposit (N tailings) to evaluate their potential as valuable materials in soils, including soil reconstruction, technosol developments, mine-site reclamation, and nutrient source in agronomic plant production. Mineralogy was analyzed using scanning electron microscope-based automated mineralogy (SEM-AM), and bulk elemental composition was determined via X-ray fluorescence (XRF). SEM-AM results show that the Fen sample is dominated by soluble carbonates (>90%), being a source of Ca, Mg, Fe, with limited contribution of P from apatite (1.4%). Rana tailings are dominated by quartz and silicates (>60%), with ∼10% carbonates and ∼10% Fe-oxides. Nussir sample, containing 37% carbonates and 7.3% biotite, offers valuable sources of Ca and Mg. XRF analysis detected trace elements of potential concern for soil ecosystems, including Mn, Ba, Sr, La, Ce, Nd in Fen sample, and Mn in Rana and Nussir samples that require further speciation and bioavailability analyses. All three materials exhibit fine particle size (C tailings <150 μm, R tailings <400 μm, N tailings <140 μm), high alkalinity (pH 9-10), and an absence of sulfide minerals, reducing the risk of acid mine drainage. Based on well-established analytical methods for mineral characterization, the findings suggest that mine tailings can potentially be recycled within the soil ecosystems as a soil amendment and nutrient source, although further studies are needed to assess element bioavailability and long-term environmental impacts.

title: Comparing the adsorption and molecular fractionation of rice straw biochar-derived and leached dissolved organic matter on iron (oxyhydr)oxides
description: Publication date: September 2026 Source: Applied Geochemistry, Volume 207 Author(s): Cuncun Xu, Tao Cao, Hao Chen, Jianzhong Song, Bin Jiang, Yin Zhong, Haiyan Song, Ping'an Peng
abstract: Iron (oxyhydr)oxides play a crucial role in regulating the biogeochemical cycling of dissolved organic matter (DOM) in natural environments. The pyrolysis of crop straw fundamentally alters the molecular composition of water-extractable organic matter, which results in distinct adsorption fractionation on iron (oxyhydr)oxides and subsequently different effects on soil DOM. Here, we investigated the adsorption and molecular fractionation of dissolved black carbon (DBC) derived from rice straw biochar and as well as leached DOM, during their adsorption onto magnetite, ferrihydrite, and hematite. Our results showed that magnetite consistently had the highest adsorption capacity for DBC and DOM, followed by ferrihydrite and then hematite, highlighting the importance of iron (oxyhydr)oxides surface properties in influencing DBC and DOM adsorption. Molecular analysis revealed pronounced selective fractionation during adsorption. Specifically, adsorption led to reductions in the O/C ratios and aromaticity indices of residual DBC as well as decreases in the O/C ratios of residual DOM, indicating that iron (oxyhydr)oxides selectively capture highly oxidized and unsaturated compounds. Furthermore, DBC showed a preference for removing CRAM- and tannin-like compounds, whereas DOM more strongly depleted carbohydrates, tannin-like compounds, and peptides. These differences imply that returning biochar to soil may encourage the accumulation of condensed aromatic structures through iron oxide adsorption, whereas returning straw may help stabilize oxygen-containing aliphatic compounds in soil DOM. Overall, these results provide new understanding of how DBC and DOM interact with iron (oxyhydr)oxides at interfaces and have important implications for carbon cycling, the transport and transformation of environmental pollutants and soil remediation efforts.

title: Definition of regional background values of trace element in soils of Castilla-La Mancha region, Spain
description: Publication date: September 2026 Source: Applied Geochemistry, Volume 207 Author(s): Iker Martínez-del-Pozo, Mónica Celina Gómez-Pachón, Sofía Rivera, Inmaculada Ferri-Moreno, Mari Luz García-Lorenzo, Saturnino Lorenzo, José Ignacio Barquero-Peralbo, Xabier Arroyo, Pablo Higueras, José María Esbrí
abstract: The present study defines geochemical threshold values (GTV) and background values (GBV), in addition to analysing of the spatial distribution of major and trace elements in uncontaminated soils in the Castilla-La Mancha (CLM) region (Spain). A total of 869 samples were analysed from the entire region by X-Ray Fluorescence to determine the presence of Ti, Cr, Mn, Fe, Ni, Cu, Zn, As, Rb, Sr, Zr, and Pb. A principal components analysis (PCA) was performed in conjunction with the observation of the regional lithology. This process resulted in the delineation of seven geochemical zones. The calculation of GTVs was undertaken using different approaches for the complete dataset and by geochemical zones (percentile-based techniques (p95 and p98); Tukey's inner fences (TIF); median+2xmedian absolute deviation (mMAD); and cumulative probability plot (CP)). The results obtained from the CP plot are considered the most robust for defining the GTVs of CLM, because of the capacity to observe subpopulations and conduct a lithological comparison of potential geochemical anomalies. In order to calculate the GBVs, outliers above the GTVs were eliminated to create geochemical interpolated maps for CLM. These maps and values were then used to make comparisons with regional, national and European references levels. The results obtained indicate significant enrichment of Ti, Mn, Fe, Zn, Zr and Pb, suggesting an association with metallogenetic districts. Elevated Rb values were identified within the granitic units, whereas Cr and Ni are strongly associated with the Campo de Calatrava volcanic field. In contrast, the Cenozoic gypsum-rich evaporitic deposits are characterised by Sr enrichment. This research enhances the existing GTV and GBV forms for CLM, providing a robust foundation for future studies in the domain of soil investigation, environmental management and land use.

title: Crop rotations modulate chemical transformation of dissolved organic matter during mineral surface-bound Fe(II) oxidation in paddy soils
description: Publication date: September 2026 Source: Applied Geochemistry, Volume 207 Author(s): Cong Wu, Fangling Li, Taoyuan Ouyang, Wei Peng, Yanqi Xiao, Fu Liu, Qihong Zhu, Na Zhang, Hao-Jie Cui, Wenjuan Liao
abstract: Fe(II)-bearing minerals oxygenation play important role in chemical mineralization and sequestration of dissolved organic matter (DOM) in paddy soils. However, the regulation of crop rotations in DOM chemical transformation during mineral surface-bound Fe(II) oxidation remains insufficiently understood. In this work, the transformations of DOM from two crop rotation paddy soils (maize-rice, MR-DOM, and soybean-rice, SR-DOM) were investigated during oxidation of surface-bound Fe(II) on goethite, alumina, and kaolinite, respectively. After oxidation of 1 mM mineral-adsorbed Fe(II) for 2 h, CO2 production in SR-DOM ranged from 42.18 to 101.18 μg C·mg−1 DOC, which was about 1.22∼1.38 times higher than that in MR-DOM. Among the minerals, alumina presented the highest CO2 release because of promoting higher •OH accumulation, whereas goethite limited CO2 generation due to strong DOM adsorption, despite enhancing Fe(II) electron utilization for •OH formation. Compared with SR-DOM, stronger adsorption of MR-DOM by minerals resulted in more effective protection of MR-DOM, from mineralization to CO2. XPS and FT-ICR-MS analyses showed that greater radical CC and C–C bond cleavage reactions occurred in SR-DOM during oxidation, and increased DOM saturation and oxidation states. In contrast to SR-DOM, MR-DOM underwent more oxygen addition reactions during oxidation, leading to an increase in molecular weight and consequently less CO2 production from •OH mineralization. These findings provide new insights into the distinct processes of carbon sequestration and mineralization during redox cycles in paddy soils with various crop rotations.

title: Hydrological convergence and surface–groundwater connectivity are associated with fluorescent groundwater DOM in the Victoria and Kyoga Basins, Uganda
description: Publication date: September 2026 Source: Applied Geochemistry, Volume 207 Author(s): Derick Muloogi, Daren C. Gooddy, David A. Polya, Laura A. Richards
abstract: Dissolved organic matter (DOM) influences subsurface biogeochemistry yet controls on its composition in many tropical sub-Saharan aquifers remain poorly understood. Here, we integrated satellite-derived land-use/land-cover (LULC) data, terrain metrics, and inorganic tracers (NO3 −/Cl−, SO4 2−/Cl−) to evaluate how LULC patterns and terrain-driven hydrological convergence, expressed as topographic wetness index (TWI), influence bulk and fluorescent groundwater DOM (fDOM) across multiple spatial scales in Uganda. Groundwater DOM was dominated by weakly aromatic, highly processed material of mixed terrestrial and microbial origin (specific ultraviolet absorbance (SUVA) 0.5, β:α < 1, and fluorescence index (FI) ∼ 1.6). Total fluorescence (0.1 – 12.3 RU; median 0.3 RU) was dominated by fulvic-like (∼35 %) and tryptophan-like (∼29 %), followed by tyrosine-like (∼18 %) and humic-like (∼17 %) components. The combined influence of LULC and TWI was scale dependent, although LULC categories showed no significant associations with groundwater DOM, except surface-water cover. TWI was positively associated with dissolved organic carbon (DOC), and fDOM components consistent with potential lateral mobilisation and surface–groundwater interaction in hydrologically convergent zones. NO3 −/Cl− ratios were negatively correlated with DOC (Spearman ρ ∼ −0.56), and positively with SUVA (ρ ∼ 0.46), consistent with preferential depletion of relatively bioavailable DOM fractions and relative enrichment of more aromatic residual DOM under nitrate-enriched conditions. These results show that in the Victoria and Kyoga basins, hydrological convergence, rather than land use alone, likely influences groundwater DOM composition, highlighting surface waters and near-surface hyporheic zones as potential sources and transformation environments for organic matter entering aquifers.

title: REE and radioelement enrichment in heavy-mineral coastal placers: An integrated geophysical–geochemical synthesis from the eastern coast of India
description: Publication date: September 2026 Source: Applied Geochemistry, Volume 207 Author(s): Shayantani Ghosal, Sudha Agrahari, Debashish Sengupta
abstract: This study presents a data integrated synthesis with new analytical results for mineral exploration along the eastern fringe of Peninsular India, focusing on heavy mineral rich coastal placer systems of Odisha. Rather than a standalone case study, the work combines previously published datasets with newly acquired field measurements and laboratory analyses to develop a unified understanding of the spatial distribution, subsurface architecture and geochemical characteristics of these placers. Non-invasive two-dimensional electrical resistivity imaging conducted along >40 km of coastline (including newly acquired profiles) delineates laterally continuous low-resistivity zones (0.1-1.1 Ω m) extending to depths of ∼20-25 m, interpreted as heavy mineral concentrations dominated by ilmenite and rutile. Near river mouths, these conductive zones occur as deeper, discontinuous pockets, reflecting localized depositional controls. Previously published radiometric datasets are integrated to the geoelectrical framework which enabled a robust multi-proxy comparison. The beach placers show elevated thorium and comparatively low uranium and potassium concentrations. Laboratory geochemical analyses, expanded through new datasets, indicate substantial enrichment of rare earth elements (REEs), with an average total REE concentration of 4243 ppm, approximately 29 times the upper continental crustal average (LREE > HREE). Inter-method comparison of REE concentrations obtained through ICP-MS and instrumental neutron activation analysis yields strong correlations (R2 = 0.6–0.8), confirming analytical robustness. A consistent positive relationship between thorium and total REE concentrations highlights the potential of thorium as an effective first-pass proxy for REE exploration. By explicitly integrating legacy datasets with new observations, this study establishes a process-based, multi-proxy exploration framework, advancing regional placer exploration models and providing an approach applicable to analogous coastal systems worldwide.

title: Transport and remobilization of Eu(III)-silicate colloids in a simulated fractured granite-groundwater system
description: Publication date: September 2026 Source: Applied Geochemistry, Volume 207 Author(s): Daming Zhang, Yujia Zhang, Qicheng Yao, Wenbo Zhang, Qiang Jin, Zongyuan Chen, Zhijun Guo
abstract: The migration of actinides (An) in deep geological repositories is significantly influenced by colloid-facilitated transport, particularly via the formation of An-silicate colloids. This study investigates the transport and release behaviors of Eu(III)-silicate colloids (used as an analog for trivalent actinides) in a simulated water-saturated granite fracture system. Transport experiments were conducted in a laboratory-scale fracture flow system to evaluate the effects of pH (7.3-8.5), ionic strength (1-400 mM), and fulvic acid (FA, 2.0-10.0 mg/L) on colloid mobility, while retention-release experiments were performed to assess their remobilization potential. Mechanisms were elucidated using size-fractionated analysis, with consideration of colloidal heterogeneity, and DLVO theory. The results indicate that Eu(III)-silicate colloids exhibit high mobility under conditions of high pH (8.5) and low ionic strength (1 mM), achieving a recovery rate of 97.9%. This enhanced transport is driven by strong electrostatic repulsion and minimized hydrodynamic size. The presence of FA further promotes mobility through steric stabilization and the formation of soluble Eu(III)-FA complexes. The transport mechanism transitions from Langmuirian blocking to ripening when Eu(III)-silicate colloids become unstable and aggregate under elevated ionic strength (e.g., >200 mM NaCl at pH 8.5). Colloidal fractions with higher Si/Eu ratios demonstrated superior transport capability due to their smaller size and stronger surface charge, indicating that the heterogeneity of Eu(III)-silicate colloids plays an important role in their transport behavior. Furthermore, retained colloids at pH 8.0 and 300 mM NaCl can be remobilized by perturbations such as decreasing ionic strength, increasing pH, or increasing flow velocity. This release process is governed by a dual mechanism involving both direct detachment from the fracture surface and the disaggregation of larger aggregates. However, prolonged retention times were found to inhibit remobilization due to the aging effect, which strengthens adhesion and leads to a transition towards more stable attachment. These findings provide critical insights into the environmental fate of An (III)-silicate colloids and emphasize the potential risks associated with their remobilization in fractured granite environments.

title: Lead isotope studies of Precambrian basement in the midcontinent United States: Implications for metal sources in Mississippi Valley-type ores
description: Publication date: September 2026 Source: Applied Geochemistry, Volume 207 Author(s): Mackenzie Moorhead, Adriana Potra, John R. Samuelsen, Gregory Dumond
abstract: Fifty-three basement samples from the Central Plains Orogen (1.65-1.8 Ga) and Southern Granite-Rhyolite Province (1.3-1.4 Ga) have been analyzed for Pb isotope ratios and for U, Th, and Pb concentrations to re-evaluate the possibility of a basement Pb source for Mississippi Valley-type (MVT) ores throughout the greater midcontinent region and to develop a schematic model pertaining to the ore-forming mechanisms. Current results for the Granite-Rhyolite Province basement rocks are all collinear with the array defined by published data and show higher Pb isotope ratios. This suggests mixing between a more depleted source, potentially a reservoir in the upper mantle, and a more enriched source that requires a crustal/sediment contribution. The Pb isotope ratios of the Central Plains Orogen rocks plot between those of the Granite-Rhyolite Province, indicating source(s) of intermediate enrichment. An important finding of this study is that several basement samples that yield highly radiogenic Pb isotope ratios (208Pb/204Pb between 40.534 and 45.810) originate from shallower depths (between around 650 m and 1050 m), and those that yield low Pb isotope ratios (208Pb/204Pb between 37.171 and 37.860) originate from deeper depths (between around 2200 m and 3800 m). While the current results agree with the description of the midcontinent basement being heterogeneous, there are likely specific, localized features (e.g., younger intrusion or a basement high) that impart certain rocks their unique, highly radiogenic Pb signatures. The samples that display the high Pb isotope ratios plot near the radiogenic end-member of the MVT ore array. The Pb isotope patterns noticed in basement rocks originating from various levels, together with available Pb isotopes and fluid inclusions data in the MVT ores, support the interpretation that metal-rich fluids emanating from local, shallower, more radiogenic basement rocks migrated along deep-seated faults directly to deposition zones, without mixing with basin-derived fluids (e.g., Northern Arkansas District). Other basement-derived fluids emanating from deeper, less radiogenic basement rocks might have migrated upward along deep-seated faults, then laterally, potentially mixing with basin-derived fluids enriched in radiogenic Pb and contributing to isotopic diversity (e.g., Tri-State and Southeast Missouri districts). The possible presence of unique features within the basement mentioned above may explain why the 1.05 Ga and 1.01 Ga model Pb source ages for midcontinent ores are younger than the ages of the Granite Rhyolite Province and the Central Plains Orogen.

title: Recognizing geochemical anomalies by locally selective combination of parallel autoencoders: Integrating AE, VAE, and AE-1SVM for robust metal exploration targeting
description: Publication date: September 2026 Source: Applied Geochemistry, Volume 207 Author(s): Zeinab Soltani, Hossein Hassani, Ardeshir Hezarkhani, Saeid Esmaeiloghli
abstract: Deep learning (DL) models have become leading techniques for recognizing mineralization-related geochemical anomalies because they can learn deep feature representations of multi-element geochemical data arising from nonlinear Earth systems and complex statistical distributions. Among different DL techniques, autoencoder-backbone models are particularly attractive for geochemical exploration because they operate in an unsupervised manner and thus bypass the practical limitations of supervised strategies that require labeled training datasets. However, a critical challenge in geochemical anomaly detection is the model-based uncertainty imposed by the fact that different autoencoder-based detectors may generate inconsistent anomaly patterns within distinct geological architectures and highly complex frequency distributions. This issue may mislead metal exploration targeting when an anomaly map derived from a single model is used to delimit target areas. To address this model-based uncertainty, in this research, we propose the locally selective combination of parallel autoencoders (LSCPAE), which integrates three autoencoder-backbone anomaly detectors—autoencoder (AE), variational autoencoder (VAE), and autoencoder-based one-class support vector machine (AE-1SVM)—through the locally selective combination of parallel outlier ensembles (LSCP) strategy. The proposed workflow is applied to the stream sediment geochemical data pertaining to the Feizabad district, NE Iran, where anomaly scores from AE, VAE, AE-1SVM, and LSCPAE models are mapped to delineate spatial patterns favorable for gold-copper exploration. Performance appraisal through success rate curves indicates that the LSCPAE-derived anomaly map delivers a superior targeting performance than stand-alone autoencoder-backbone scenarios and soft voting technique (as a global ensemble strategy). The results suggest that the LSCPAE model can effectively reduce model-based uncertainty and provide lower-risk grounds for further metal exploration.

title: Historical fluxes and enrichment factors of trace elements in Lake Erie sediments
description: Publication date: September 2026 Source: Applied Geochemistry, Volume 207 Author(s): Mahsa Tashakor, Anthony Chappaz
abstract: The Lake Erie watershed, the most densely populated of the Laurentian Great Lakes, has experienced significant trace element (TE) contamination over the past two centuries due to industrialization, agriculture, and urbanization. This study examines the sedimentary profiles of cadmium, chromium, copper, antimony, tungsten and zinc in a sediment core from the Central Basin of Lake Erie to reconstruct historical fluxes and enrichment factors for all these TEs in relation to anthropogenic impacts on the lake's watershed over the last century. Using 210Pb geochronology and 137Cs activity, sediment mass accumulation rates were determined, revealing that the Central Basin experienced the highest sediment loading among the Great Lakes during the second half of the 20th century. This coincides with increased TE inputs probably driven by industrial activities, fossil fuel combustion, and land-use changes. We identified four distinct periods of TE fluxes: (1) pre-1900, with minimal anthropogenic influence; (2) early to mid-1900s, characterized by rapid industrialization and a sharp rise in TE concentrations; (3) 1950s to 1990, marked by ongoing industrial and agricultural contamination; and (4) 1990–2014, when regulatory efforts contributed to a substantial decline in TE levels. Yet the levels of Sn and W in the top sediments remain concerning. Industrial processes were the primary source of TE contamination, and we present new evidence linking W contamination to historical tungsten production in the region. These findings underscore the lasting environmental impact of human activities on Lake Erie's sediments and emphasize the need for continued and improved monitoring and mitigation.

title: Environmental controls on methyl tert -butyl ether (MTBE) interphase redistribution in compacted low-permeability soils
description: Publication date: September 2026 Source: Applied Geochemistry, Volume 207 Author(s): Meng Wang, Kangping Cui, Long Xu, Fusheng Zha, Qiao Wang, Jinkun Huang, Jingjing Liu
abstract: Methyl tert-butyl ether (MTBE), a volatile and relatively water-soluble LNAPL compound, can partition into free, dissolved, vapor, and adsorbed states after release; however, quantitative evidence for how environmental controls drive redistribution in low-permeability soils remains limited. This study develops a sequential multi-phase NAPL extraction and analysis framework to quantify MTBE interphase distribution in compacted soils subjected to controlled thermal, hygroscopic, and compaction conditions. The method enables direct quantification of all four phase reservoirs, allowing phase-specific evaluation of environmental impacts on interphase redistribution. Across the full range of conditions tested, the vapor phase accounted for nearly all contaminant mass, whereas free phase accumulation was thermodynamically unfavorable under the tested conditions. Adsorbed and dissolved fractions acted as environmentally responsive reservoirs that were systematically displaced toward the vapor domain, indicating that vapor management governs mass reduction in compacted low-permeability matrices. Interphase redistribution showed strong directional responses, increasing temperature suppressed adsorbed and dissolved fractions through desorption, volatilization, and strengthened gas-water partitioning; rising relative humidity reduced sorption and expanded aqueous retention; and increasing dry density restricted pore water connectivity and favored gas-associated storage. Machine learning analysis confirmed temperature as the dominant driver of adsorbed phase behavior, while dissolved phase variability depended jointly on temperature, humidity, and dry density, revealing marked non-additive interactions. Molecular simulations corroborated weakened adsorption affinity, moisture-enhanced diffusion pathways, and confinement-regulated mobility, providing nanoscale evidence for desorption-controlled phase evolution. The combined experimental, modeling, and molecular results provide a mechanistic basis for designing MTBE remediation strategies in low-permeability source zones, especially those emphasizing vapor-phase removal and environmental regulation. Extension to other LNAPL compounds should consider compound-specific differences in volatility, aqueous solubility, and hydrophobicity.

title: Effect of clays on the formation kinetics of xonotlite
description: Publication date: September 2026 Source: Applied Geochemistry, Volume 207 Author(s): S. Mingione, F. Winnefeld, J. Mareels, P. Lopez, B. Lothenbach
abstract: Xonotlite (Ca6Si6O17(OH)2) formation is highly dependent on the reactivity of the raw materials used during hydrothermal synthesis. The raw materials, typically silica (SiO2) and lime (CaO), often contain secondary phases such as clay and Mg-bearing compounds which can further influence the synthesis of xonotlite. While small amounts of Mg stabilize xonotlite, the role of clay which may introduce Al, Fe and Si, remains poorly understood. This study investigates the impact of different quantities of clay during xonotlite synthesis. Xonotlite was obtained through hydrothermal synthesis carried out in an autoclave with stirring at 180 °C. The reaction kinetics was studied by stopping the synthesis at different time intervals and analyzing the obtained solids by XRD, TGA and FT-IR. Results indicate that the presence of aluminum from clay delays xonotlite formation and promotes instead the crystallization of (Al-)tobermorite, as confirmed by thermodynamic modelling. The effect increases with increasing quantities of clay or aluminum.

title: Cesium sorption onto clays from different deposits: experiments and modeling
description: Publication date: September 2026 Source: Applied Geochemistry, Volume 207 Author(s): Irina R. Menshikova-Tonyan, Anna S. Semenkova, Ivan Mikheev, Andrey S. Toropov, Valentina S. Svitelman, Sergey V. Zakusin, Victoria V. Krupskaya, Anna Yu. Romanchuk, Stepan N. Kalmykov
abstract: Sorption properties of clays play a crucial role in the long-term safety of radioactive waste disposal. In this study, the sorption behavior of cesium on 11 different clay samples from various geological deposits was investigated under a broad range of experimental conditions, including varying cesium concentrations and pH levels. While smectite is the predominant mineral in all samples, sorption isotherms exhibit at least two types of sorption sites with different affinities. Experimental data were analyzed using previously published thermodynamic models and their modifications, with an automated heuristic optimization approach applied to adjust model parameters. The two-site ion-exchange model demonstrated a good fit to the experimental data, yet no clear correlation was observed between the number of exchange sites and sample properties such as mineral composition, specific surface area, cation exchange capacity determined by the Cu-trien method, or layer charge. Even highly smectitic bentonites required the introduction of highly selective sorption sites to adequately describe cesium sorption behavior. These findings highlight the complexity of cesium sorption mechanisms in clays and the necessity for further studies to refine predictive models for nuclear waste management applications.

title: Groundwater pH buffering in carbonate aquifers exposed to high-calcium ash backfill
description: Publication date: September 2026 Source: Applied Geochemistry, Volume 207 Author(s): Madis Osjamets, Martin Liira, Riho Mõtlep
abstract: High-calcium ashes are known to produce highly alkaline leachates in laboratory settings, which has raised concerns regarding potential groundwater impacts when such ashes are used in mine backfills. In this study, we evaluated the effect of a high-calcium oil-shale ash backfill on groundwater pH in carbonate aquifers using an integrated approach combining geochemical modelling with a two-year field experiment. The backfill was injected into an abandoned mine drift in northeastern Estonia, and groundwater was monitored using continuous automatic sensors complemented by periodic sampling. Laboratory leaching tests confirmed the ash backfill has the potential to increase leachate pH values to above 12.5. However, geochemical modelling predicted rapid attenuation of alkalinity through buffering by bicarbonate in the carbonate aquifer, resulting in only minor pH changes restricted to the immediate vicinity of the backfill. Field observations corroborated the model predictions, showing no significant increase in pH in monitoring wells located 10 m from the backfill body. Instead of pH elevation, the most notable geochemical response in groundwater was an increase in sulphate concentrations. The results demonstrate that carbonate aquifers possess a strong natural buffering capacity that effectively mitigates the high alkalinity introduced by high-calcium ash backfill leachate. Although based on a single field site and therefore not directly generalisable to all carbonate mining settings, our results indicate that high-calcium industrial byproducts may be reused for mine reclamation with limited pH effects, while SO4 2− enrichment emerged as the dominant groundwater response. Future backfilling operations should account for the potential increase in dissolved SO4 2− in adjacent groundwater and incorporate sulphate-focused monitoring and mitigation measures into the design.

title: Hydrogeochemistry and dissolved organic matter as support tracers of recharge, flow paths, and discharge processes in hydrological systems
description: Publication date: September 2026 Source: Applied Geochemistry, Volume 207 Author(s): P.G. Schroeter, F. Bécher Quinodóz, E. Arbeloa, V. Lutri, M.C. Diéguez, P.E. García, S. Prámparo, Z. Fernández, M.T. Blarasin
abstract: This study evaluates the role of dissolved organic matter (DOM) as a tracer of hydrogeological processes in a fluvio–aeolian system of southern Córdoba, Argentina, integrating optical DOM properties with hydrochemistry. Groundwater from an unconfined aquifer, river water, and a shallow lagoon were analyzed to assess the relationships between water composition, DOM characteristics, and hydrological setting. Water mineralization is primarily controlled by water–sediment interactions, including silicate weathering, carbonate dissolution, and cation exchange. In contrast, DOM exhibits systematic variations related to source, degree of processing, and residence time. Groundwater contains moderately processed and variably humified DOM, reflecting transport within the aquifer under heterogeneous residence times, whereas river water is characterized by fresher, biologically influenced DOM associated with rapid renewal. Lagoon waters show highly humified and refractory DOM consistent with longer residence times and discharge conditions. Multivariate statistical analysis (PCA and HCA) reveals coherent patterns linking hydrochemical evolution and DOM composition, allowing differentiation of recharge, groundwater flow, and discharge sectors within the system. These results demonstrate that DOM provides complementary information to hydrochemistry and acts as a sensitive indicator of biogeochemical processing along flow paths in lowland environments.

title: Resolving barium matrix interferences in rare earth element analysis of seep barites: Implications for europium anomalies and fluid sources
description: Publication date: September 2026 Source: Applied Geochemistry, Volume 207 Author(s): Tongtong Bai, Xudong Wang, Lanlan Zhang, Zhaoyang Wang, Zice Jia, Dong Feng
abstract: Barite is an important archive for tracing fluid-rock interactions in marine systems. However, accurate determination of rare earth elements (REEs) in barite by ICP-MS is strongly hindered by polyatomic ion interferences derived from high barium (Ba) matrix, particularly affecting europium (Eu) measurements. This analytical limitation has restricted the application of REE geochemistry in studies of barites from seeps (hereafter seep barites). Here we investigate barite-carbonate pairs from seeps in the Gulf of Mexico and develop a robust analytical protocol for reliable REE determination. The procedure integrates (1) selective removal of carbonate phases by mild acetic acid leaching, (2) complete digestion of the purified barite fraction using a mixed HNO3–HF–HClO4 acid system, and (3) efficient separation of Ba from REEs using DGA resin chromatography prior to ICP-MS analysis. Comparison of REE data before and after Ba removal demonstrates that extremely positive Eu anomalies observed in untreated samples (Eu/Eu∗ up to 122) may result from BaO+/BaOH+ interferences, highlighting the importance of careful matrix separation for reliable Eu determination. After matrix separation, the barite samples display moderate positive Eu anomalies (Eu/Eu∗ = 1.25–3.85), consistent negative Ce anomalies, and heavy REE-enriched patterns. These corrected REE signatures indicate precipitation from pore fluids interacting with surrounding sediments under suboxic to oxic conditions, rather than from high temperature hydrothermal fluids. Our results suggest that some previously reported extreme Eu anomalies in barite, particularly where Ba removal or interference correction was not documented, may warrant careful re-evaluation as potential analytical artifacts, and emphasize the necessity of matrix separation for reliable REE analysis in Ba-rich minerals.

title: Hydrochar-Amended bioreactors for passive treatment of acid mine drainage
description: Publication date: September 2026 Source: Applied Geochemistry, Volume 207 Author(s): Aliching Marma, Natalie Kruse Daniels, Nigel Daniels
abstract: This study was based on a batch bioreactor experiment to investigate the effectiveness of using hydrochar as an amendment to promote the growth of sulfate-reducing bacteria (SRB) in acid mine drainage (AMD) treatment, with a primary focus on Copper (Cu), Zinc (Zn) and Cadmium (Cd) removal. This study evaluated the effect of hydrochar amendment in reducing bioreactors utilizing a mixture of organic substrates such as cow manure, maple woodchips, and cornflour acquired from a local granary, blended with hydrochar in triplicate, varying the amount of hydrochar: 0%, 5%, 10%, and 20% of the total volume in the bioreactors. Bioreactors were operated for 98 days, and water quality parameters (pH, ORP, sulfate, total sulfur, metal concentration, COD) were analyzed periodically to determine the effect of variation in bioreactor substrate. Additionally, 16S rRNA sequencing was used to determine the presence of SRB in the bioreactors at the end of the tests. The results suggested that bioreactors without hydrochar content performed better in raising pH and removing metals, likely as metal sulfides, with removal percentages of Cu (89–100%), Zn (97–100%), Cd (100%), and sulfate (50–100%), following the removal trend of Cd > Zn > Cu. Statistical analysis results demonstrated no significant influence of hydrochar on metal removal (p > 0.05), but time had a significant effect (p < 0.05), indicating that removal effectiveness improved with time regardless of hydrochar quantity. The presence of SRB was confirmed in all bioreactors, although their relative abundance varied across treatments.

title: Can river chemistry in a karst region under human influences be used for catchment rock weathering estimation?
description: Publication date: September 2026 Source: Applied Geochemistry, Volume 207 Author(s): Yan Liu, Y. Jun Xu, Xingxing Cao, Guangxi Long, Pan Wu, Zhangxing Liu
abstract: River chemistry is commonly used to estimate the weathering-induced carbon sink from rocks. However, the reliability of this approach in urbanized and agricultural watersheds remains unclear, particularly within fragile karst systems. This study examines the spatiotemporal variations in water chemistry of karst rivers across three catchments with different land use/land cover types in southwestern China. Our results reveal that rivers draining urban and agricultural catchments exhibit higher ionic loads of K+, Na+, and Cl− coupled with perturbed dissolved inorganic carbon dynamics, underscoring the influence of human activities on fluvial carbon fluxes. Especially, wastewater inputs substantially increase the concentrations of major ions (e.g., Na+, Cl−, NO3 −) and reduce ionic ratios such as Ca2+/Na+, Mg2+/Na+, and HCO3 −/Na+, shifting the river chemical signatures toward silicate weathering end-members, despite negligible actual silicate contribution, and the effect is modulated by rainfall. Such anthropogenic interference can bias assessments of natural weathering end-members and carbon source apportionment. Furthermore, nitrification in wastewater from urban and agricultural activities generates exogenous acids that participate in carbonate rock dissolution. Coupled with deviations in carbon source allocation, these processes affect the assessment of the rock weathering carbon sink. These findings highlight the need to account for anthropogenic inputs when evaluating karst carbon sink in urban and agricultural watersheds.

title: Microscopic and spectroscopic insights into uranium speciation and mobilization pathways associated with carnotite weathering in sediments
description: Publication date: September 2026 Source: Applied Geochemistry, Volume 207 Author(s): Martina Wiejski-López, Gonzalo L. Bia, Eduardo D. Wannaz, Laura Borgnino
abstract: The speciation and mobility of uranium (U) in sediments are influenced by biogeochemical factors such as redox conditions, microbial activity, and the presence of organic matter (OM) and mineral phases. This study investigates the mechanisms controlling U behavior in sediments from the Punilla Valley (Córdoba, Argentina), using an integrated suite of analytical techniques including pXRF, XRD, SEM-EDS, XPS, and XAS. Field observations, together with geochemical and mineralogical analyses, indicate that U–V mineralization (i.e., carnotite) is heterogeneously distributed within reddish pelitic sediments and occurs as coatings on carbonates, micas, and plant roots. Grain-size and compositional data show U enrichment in fine sediment fractions, reflecting remobilization and secondary concentration under supergene conditions. Uranium redistribution appears to occur through the dissolution of carnotite, followed by interactions with plant roots and authigenic carbonates, as well as partial reduction to U(IV) mediated by Fe-bearing micas and dissolved organic matter. Synchrotron-based XAS analyses indicate that U(VI) is associated with calcite, whereas both U(IV) and U(VI) are associated with Fe-bearing micas, organic matter, and plant roots. These results demonstrate active U mobilization from carnotite, likely due to meteoric water infiltration, and highlight the important role of inorganic and organic sediment components as secondary sinks controlling U dynamics in sedimentary basins.

title: Crushed fines from basic rocks of the Serra Geral Group as the sole substrate for assessing bioweathering and nutrient release in elephant grass cultivation ( Cenchrus purpureus )
description: Publication date: September 2026 Source: Applied Geochemistry, Volume 207 Author(s): Simone Zwirtes, Cassiana R.L. Michelin, Carlos Augusto Sommer, Andrea Sander, Carlos Augusto Posser Silveira
abstract: Tropical agriculture, generally developed on acid and leached soils, is highly dependent on soluble synthetic fertilizers (SSF), highlighting the need for local, economically viable, and more sustainable alternatives. Although intensive agriculture has increased global productivity through the use of these inputs, inadequate replacement of secondary nutrients and micronutrients has contributed to the progressive depletion of soil nutrients. In this context, agrogeology, particularly through the use of silicate agrominerals (SiA), emerges as a promising approach to assist developing countries in reducing their dependence on imported SSF by promoting the use of regional geological resources, such as crusher fines (CF) generated in the aggregate production chain for civil construction. This study evaluated nutrient release and plant uptake from CF derived from basic rocks of the Serra Geral Group (basalt and diabase), using an agronomic trial in which CF were used as the sole substrate, without soil addition. Elephant grass (cultivar BRS Kurumi) was grown with and without organic matter (OM) over 182 days in a greenhouse experiment arranged in a 2 × 2 factorial design, in addition to a control treatment.Reductions in Ca, Mg, K, and Si contents were observed in CF from plant treatments, more pronounced in the presence of OM, and were accompanied by substantial increases in nutrient uptake by elephant grass (up to 6.5-fold for basalt and 6-fold for diabase with OM) and in shoot dry matter (5.1 to 5.8-fold). The higher proportion of fine fractions in basalt CF favored nutrient release compared to diabase.The results indicate that bioweathering, driven by plant–OM interactions, intensified mineral dissolution and short-term release of K, Ca, Mg, Fe, and Si over months, supporting the use of CF from the studied lithologies as silicate agrominerals. The integration of SiA, plants, and OM increases biological activity, intensifies mineral dissolution in CF, and enhances agronomic efficiency, representing a viable strategy to reduce dependence on SSF in tropical agricultural systems.

title: Glucose promotes iron bi-directional redox transformation mediated by a single strain Comamonas sp. HJ-2
description: Publication date: September 2026 Source: Applied Geochemistry, Volume 207 Author(s): Rong Peng, Rui Yang, Yuhang Liang, Haichuan Sun, Hui Liu
