abstract: In anaerobic underground environments, the iron redox cycle is fundamentally driven by microbial activities, wherein the metabolic capacity of individual strains plays a pivotal role. This study investigated the regulatory mechanisms of three carbon sources — acetate, glucose, and lactate — on the iron redox cycle mediated by Comamonas sp. HJ-2 under neutral pH anaerobic conditions in Fe(III)–Fe(II) coexisting and Fe(III)-free systems. The results demonstrated that glucose enhanced Fe(II) bio-oxidation and Fe(III) bio-reduction by promoting energy metabolism. Glucose promoted sustained FMN accumulation, which is consistent with a potential contribution of the glycolysis-pentose phosphate pathway-riboflavin synthesis axis, which accumulated to a final concentration of approximately 0.40 μM. The accumulated FMN may function as an electron shuttle and thereby contribute to Fe(III) reduction. Mineralogical analyses further showed system-dependent effects of glucose. In ferrihydrite-containing systems, glucose inhibited the transformation of ferrihydrite toward more crystalline iron phases, whereas in ferrihydrite-free systems it shifted the product distribution toward a higher proportion of ferrihydrite and a lower proportion of lepidocrocite. Glucose also increased the content of surface-bound Fe(II) on minerals. In conclusion, glucose emerged as the most effective carbon source for optimizing the HJ-2-driven iron redox coupling process, likely due to its association with enhanced energy metabolism, FMN accumulation, and altered mineral phase transformation. This study elucidates the carbon source-dependent mechanisms governing microbial iron cycling in anaerobic environments and highlights the critical role of carbon source selection in enhancing iron biotransformation efficiency.

title: Fluid inclusion effects on boron isotope fractionation during halite crystallization
description: Publication date: September 2026 Source: Applied Geochemistry, Volume 207 Author(s): Xuehai Ma, Huaide Cheng, Qingyu Hai, Wenhua Han, Haizhou Ma
abstract: Salt lakes are highly sensitive to climate fluctuations, making them valuable archives of past environmental changes. Among the various geochemical proxies used to reconstruct paleoclimate, the boron isotopic composition of evaporite minerals has emerged as a powerful tool for tracking brine salinity variations. Currently, carbonates in evaporites are the primary carriers for boron isotopic composition analysis due to their relatively high boron content. However, carbonates only exist during the initial stages of salt lake evaporation, occur in limited quantities, and are difficult to separate as single minerals, introducing significant uncertainties in reconstructing paleoclimate evolution. Given the presence of halite throughout nearly all stages of salt lake evolution, its boron isotopic record holds great potential for investigating global climate change. However, the exceptionally low partition coefficient of boron in halite has sparked ongoing debate regarding the incorporation mechanisms of boron in halite and the processes governing boron isotope fractionation between brine and halite. To address these uncertainties, this study examines the boron isotopic composition of halite precipitated from evaporation experiments using underground brine from the Wuyunbulake Salt Lake (Kumish Basin, Xinjiang) alongside experiments with pure sodium chloride solutions and simulated natural samples. Our results reveal that residual fluid trapped within halite plays a crucial role in boron isotope fractionation. When halite contains residual brine, the boron fractionation factor αhalite-brine approaches 1, indicating negligible fractionation. In contrast, when halite is free of residual brine, the fractionation factor falls below 1. These findings offer new insights into boron isotope behavior in evaporative systems and strengthen the application of halite as a paleoclimate proxy.

title: A Sobol-based ensemble framework for integrating multi-method geochemical anomaly detection
description: Publication date: September 2026 Source: Applied Geochemistry, Volume 207 Author(s): Zohre Hoseinzade, Mobin Saremi, Moslem Fatehi, Amin Beiranvand Pour
abstract: In geochemical exploration, the geochemical anomalies identified by applying different methods within a study area often show considerable divergence and differences in terms of spatial distribution. Combining results from various methods across a region is challenging but crucial for producing reliable geochemical maps that help locate mineralized areas. To address this, the Sobol method was adopted to integrate the outputs of seven individual methods, including Isolation Forest (IF), Autoencoder (AE), Variational autoencoder (VAE), AE-one class support vector machine (AE1SVM), Deep One-Class Classification (Deep SVD), Cook's distance (CD), and Copula-based outlier detection (COPOD). To investigate the efficiency of the proposed approach, the Moalleman region located in NE Iran was selected as the real-case study. After that, the individual models were combined using a novel Sobol-based approach in which pseudo-random numbers were generated through quasi-Monte Carlo sampling. Then, a suitable statistical criterion was defined to identify and select the most stable weighted combination, and the final ensemble map was binarized using a percentile threshold. The identified anomalies through the Sobol approach show strong spatial correlation with known mineral occurrences (KMOs), major fault systems, and favorable lithological units. The proposed Sobol-based ensemble modeling framework effectively reduces model-related uncertainty and enhances the reliability of multi-element geochemical anomaly detection. Its demonstrated capacity to integrate diverse anomaly detection methods provides a robust decision-support tool for mineral exploration programs. The results underscore the approach's potential for delineating polymetallic mineralization targets and guiding future exploration in data-scarce or geologically complex regions.

title: Corrosion of borosilicate glass under unsaturated conditions: temperature-dependent evolution of secondary phases and surface alteration layer
description: Publication date: September 2026 Source: Applied Geochemistry, Volume 207 Author(s): Yuhan Jiao, Xuan Wang, Wenxu Yin, Junjiang Zhu, Zhentao Zhang, Laurent Charlet, Qi Sun, Kaifeng Wang
abstract: Predicting the long-term performance of borosilicate glass for nuclear waste immobilization under unsaturated repository conditions requires a fundamental understanding of the evolution of the surface alteration layer (SAL) and secondary phases during corrosion. In this study, long-term static leaching experiments (up to 760 d, 50-90 °C) were conducted in pre-equilibrated solutions to investigate the corrosion behavior of borosilicate glass under unsaturated conditions. The evolution of aqueous chemistry, secondary phases, and the SAL was characterized using solution analysis combined with XRD, SEM, and STEM techniques. The results show that B release increases continuously with temperature and reaction time, whereas dissolved Si initially increases and subsequently exhibits slight variations associated with SAL evolution and secondary phase precipitation. XRD and SEM analyses reveal the progressive formation of secondary phases on the glass surface, including zeolites, analcime, calcium silicate, smectite, and barite. STEM-EDS observations further demonstrate that the SAL develops a multilayer structure consisting of a relatively dense inner alteration layer, a porous outer alteration region, and a compositional gradient region near the glass-SAL interface. These findings provide new insights into the coupled processes controlling borosilicate glass durability and improve the basis for performance assessment of vitrified nuclear waste in geological disposal environments.

title: Lead exposure in an urban population: isotopic evidence reveals contributions from dietary and inhalation pathways
description: Publication date: September 2026 Source: Applied Geochemistry, Volume 207 Author(s): Shuhui Mu, Jin Wu, Jiaxin Ye, Jiemin Liu, Guangle Qiu, Xiaoyuan Lin, Xiangyang Bi
abstract: Environmental lead (Pb) exposure remains a persistent global public health concern. Dietary intake is widely recognized as the predominant exposure pathway, while the contribution of inhalation of Pb-containing particles to elevated blood lead levels (BLLs) has not been adequately explored. This study analyzed BLLs and lead isotopic fingerprints of residents in Guiyang, a typical city in Southwest China, and compared them with dietary samples, environmental media, and major lead emission sources to identify the primary sources and exposure pathways of lead in local residents. The results reveal strikingly elevated BLLs in both adults (57.8 μg/L) and children (44.0 μg/L), which are markedly higher than the U.S. national reference values (35 μg/L). A clear age-dependent trend was also observed, with BLLs generally increasing with age. The IsoSource model based on lead isotopic signatures revealed that lead in residents' blood primarily originated from lead-zinc smelting emissions (29.7%), historical vehicle emissions (29.5%), current traffic emissions (24.9%), and coal combustion emissions (15.9%). Furthermore, lead isotopic signatures showed that dietary intake and inhalation were the two major exposure pathways, with a binary mixing model estimating their relative contributions as 45.3% and 54.7%, respectively. This study demonstrates that lead isotope fingerprinting is a powerful tool for tracing environmental lead sources and human exposure routes, providing essential complementary insights to conventional exposure assessment models. These findings underscore the importance of integrated public health strategies that address both inhalation and dietary pathways to effectively mitigate lead exposure risks.

title: Disentangling the controls on fossil bone geochemistry using partial redundancy analysis
description: Publication date: September 2026 Source: Applied Geochemistry, Volume 207 Author(s): Michał P. Surowski, Krzysztof Owocki, Bogusław Bagiński, David Chew, Foteini Drakou
abstract: Bones undergo severe diagenesis after burial, which leads to significant changes in their geochemistry during fossilization. There are many factors that influence the final composition of a fossilized bone, including the local burial conditions (further called the locality), cortical thickness, and skeletal part. In this study, we used partial redundancy analysis (pRDA) to investigate how these factors influence the geochemical composition of dinosaur bones from the Nemegt and Djadokhta Formations from the Gobi Desert (southern Mongolia). Four pRDA models were created to estimate the impact of these factors (locality, cortical thickness and skeletal part) on bone geochemistry. The results demonstrate that all of these factors exhibit statistically significant impact on bone geochemistry. The most significant factor is the locality. The elements most applicable for differentiating between localities are the medium to heavy rare earth elements (REE). Cortical thickness is a more significant factor than the skeletal part. Despite this, when cortical thickness and skeletal parts were analysed together, the thinnest bones and tibiae proved to have the largest impact on the model. Thinner bones are usually more enriched in REE and especially in heavy REE. This relationship becomes less clear with increasing thickness due to potential mechanical damage during diagenesis. The thicker bones tend to prefer Zn, Sr, Ba, and U over REE during diagenesis. The results also show that tibiae contain relatively more Ca than other bones, which may be related to their resistance to diagenetic processes.

title: A GIXAFS study of the Fe oxide precipitates on quartz surfaces
description: Publication date: September 2026 Source: Applied Geochemistry, Volume 207 Author(s): Francesco Di Benedetto, Giordano Montegrossi, Francesco d’Acapito, Massimo Innocenti, Maurizio Romanelli
abstract: This study investigates the interaction between quartz surfaces and iron-bearing solutions through the precipitation of Fe oxide phases under controlled physicochemical conditions. Three differently oriented quartz crystal surfaces were exposed to buffered and unbuffered Fe(II) and Fe(III) solutions, and the resulting surface precipitates were analysed by GIXAFS spectroscopy. Due to the extremely low amount of deposited material, GIXAFS represented the only suitable technique capable of simultaneously probing iron oxidation state and local structural arrangement. The results demonstrate that Fe precipitates as nanoscale clusters rather than continuous surface coatings, independently of the crystallographic orientation of the quartz substrate. XANES, pre-edge, and EXAFS analyses reveal that the final Fe speciation frequently differs from the nominal redox state imposed by the starting solutions, with widespread occurrence of mixed Fe(II)–Fe(III) species and hematite-like local structures. Thermodynamic modelling performed with PHREEQC and Pourbaix diagrams successfully explains part of the observed behaviour, particularly the tendency toward Fe(III) oxide formation during evaporation and maturation of the precipitates. However, some experimental observations, including unexpected redox transformations, cannot be fully accounted for by bulk thermodynamics alone, suggesting an additional contribution from quartz surface effects or surface defects. These findings provide new insights into Fe oxide nucleation and redox evolution on silica surfaces, with potential implications for geochemical processes, environmental remediation, and the reactivity of crystalline silica in biological environments. In particular, the observed mixed-valence Fe precipitates may represent an additional contribution to the complex mechanistic framework linking crystalline silica exposure, persistent oxidative stress, and silica-related lung diseases.

title: Behaviour of 15 non-REE trace elements in Late Triassic vertebrate fossils: new insights into incorporation mechanisms and palaeoenvironmental proxy potentials
description: Publication date: September 2026 Source: Applied Geochemistry, Volume 207 Author(s): Aishee Sanyal, Sanghamitra Ray
abstract: Trace elements, usually present in negligible amounts in natural systems and living organisms, often show elevated concentrations in fossil remains due to diagenetic uptake. Concentrations of 15 non-rare earth elements (REE) (Be, Sc, Co, Ga, Rb, Sr, Y, Zr, Nb, Cs, Ba, Hf, Pb, Th, and U) were analysed in fossil bones and associated host rocks from the Upper Triassic Tiki Formation, India to document for the first time measurable concentrations of elements such as Be and Ga. Overall trace element distribution patterns in the fossils and host rocks indicate comparable diagenetic conditions, though relatively higher concentrations in the former are interpreted to reflect enrichment primarily from diagenetic fluids rather than surrounding sediments. Enrichment factor (EF) calculations highlight significant enrichment of Sr, Y, Ba, and U in fossils (EF > 1), reflecting incorporation through Ca2+ substitution in apatite and adsorption into pore spaces during fluid-mediated diagenesis. In contrast, Be, Sc, Co, Ga, Rb, Zr, Nb, Cs, Hf, Pb, and Th yield EF values < 1, suggesting retention within detrital mineral phases. Several elements such as Co and Pb acted as redox indicators, with low Th/U ratios and modest U concentrations suggesting localised reducing microenvironments formed by organic matter decay. Principal Component Analysis further supports the dominating influence of fluid-mediated and lithogenic inputs on trace-element distribution in the Tiki bonebeds. Elevated Sr and Ba concentrations together with host rock Sr/Cu and Rb/Sr ratios suggest deposition under a seasonally variable semi-arid climatic regime. This study represents one of the first comprehensive investigations of non-REE trace elements in fossil bones, demonstrating their independent significance relative to REEs in reconstructing diagenetic palaeoenvironments, provenance, and palaeoclimatic conditions.

title: Relative Kinetics of Precipitation of Barium Chromate and Barite in Groundwater
description: Publication date: Available online 5 August 2026 Source: Applied Geochemistry Author(s): Abhas Singh, Mainak Bhattacharya, Ashwini Kumar Mohapatra
abstract: Water-soluble and carcinogenic hexavalent chromium [Cr(VI)] poses serious health risks due to its potential migration in aquifers and interaction with naturally present barium [Ba] to form sparingly soluble colloidal barium chromate [BaCrO4(s)]. However, Ba may also react with other solutes predominantly present in many groundwaters like dissolved sulfate [SO4], causing precipitation of barite [BaSO4(s)]. The eventual fate of Cr(VI) in such groundwaters may be governed by the relative rates of formation of these two solids, which are currently not known. In this contribution, simultaneous formation of BaCrO4(s) and BaSO4(s) in groundwater matrix and their relative kinetics were investigated through continuous flow stirred tank reactor experiments. Chromium-free Ba-spiked SO4-containing groundwater was introduced into the reactor, preloaded with Ba-free Cr(VI)-spiked SO4-containing groundwater, at a flow rate of 0.2 mL min-1. Aqueous samples were collected with time and analyzed for Cr(VI), SO4, Ba, and pH till steady-state was attained. Geochemical analysis of solute data and characterization of the precipitated solids confirmed rapid formation of a solid solution of ∼86 mol% BaCrO4(s) and ∼14 mol% BaSO4(s). Solution saturation indices with respect to BaCrO4(s) gradually decreased over time, but persistent supersaturation with BaSO4(s) suggested conditions favorable for formation of BaSO4(s). Time-dependent Cr(VI), SO4, and Ba concentrations were modelled with process-based mass balance equations. Optimized surface area normalized precipitation rate constants of BaCrO4(s) and BaSO4(s) were obtained as 5.0-6.2×10-8 mol m-2 s-1 and 1.3×10-8 mol m-2 s-1, respectively, indicating that BaCrO4(s) precipitates approximately four times faster than BaSO4(s). Determination of these constants would help in accurate prediction of Cr(VI) transport in contaminated aquifers rich in Ba and possibly similar co-solutes.

title: Uranium remobilization from a riparian wetland: Implications on long-term stewardship and extreme rain events
description: Publication date: Available online 5 August 2026 Source: Applied Geochemistry Author(s): Daniel I. Kaplan, Karah M. Greene, Wei Xing, Arelis M. Rivera-Giboyeaux, Kenneth M. Kemner, Peng Lin
abstract: Natural attenuation of contaminants by wetlands can cause them to become secondary sources of contamination. The objectives of this field study were to: 1) measure the remobilization of uranium (U) in a stream flowing through a contaminated wetland in South Carolina, USA, and 2) develop empirical relationships between rainfall and U remobilization. Stream water was sampled hourly during six storm events ranging from 0.69 to 9.87 cm of rainfall, which caused flow to increase by as much as 1100% with respect to base flow. Uranium concentrations in all filtered samples, U<0.45μm, were below the Maximum Contaminant Limit of 30 μg/L U. Conversely, as much as 94 vol% of the U in stream samples (g U/L streamwater) was associated with suspended solids, U≥0.45μm. Consequently, significant correlations (p < 0.01) existed between stream water total U and suspended solids concentrations (or turbidity). Using a linear relationship (p < 0.01) between rainfall and remobilized U (g-U/sampling-event), it was estimated that 29% of the remobilized U in the year 2024 occurred during the three days of greatest rainfall. Similarly, using historical rainfall data, it was estimated that 864 kg-U, or 2.2% of the original 43,500 kg-U released into the wetland 55 years ago had been remobilized. This value of remobilized U is consistent with U-mass balance at the study site. Predictions of increased regional total rainfall and the number of extreme rainfall events may increase the rate of contaminant dispersion from riparian systems.

title: Differential Responses of Vanadate Reduction to Soil Aggregate Types
description: Publication date: Available online 5 August 2026 Source: Applied Geochemistry Author(s): Zhenhan Li, Song Wang, Fengyuan Zhuang, Qinghao Zhang, Baogang Zhang
abstract: Different soil aggregate fractions create distinct biogeochemical microhabitats, driving divergent ecological adaptations and functional traits. In this study, different aggregate fractions from a vanadium-contaminated soil were inoculated into the reactors to evaluate their differences in pentavalent vanadium [V(V)] reduction capacity. Micro-aggregates (MiA) achieved the highest V(V) removal efficiency of 96.2 ± 0.12% and the fastest first-order removal kinetics (rate constant 0.06 h-1), followed by small aggregates, medium aggregates, and large aggregates. The microbial consortia from aggregate could transform toxic soluble V(V) into less mobile tetravalent vanadium [V(IV)] precipitates, thereby contributing to the remediation of vanadium-contaminated soil. During the V(V) reduction process, microbial communities underwent significant changes, exhibiting lower richness and diversity and forming a distinct cluster compared to the initial samples. Meanwhile, the relative abundance of metal-reducing genera increased from 5.29 ± 0.79% to 39.2 ± 12.3%. Co-occurrence network analysis revealed tight microbial collaboration, whereas larger aggregate fractions were associated with lower V(V) removal efficiency. Metagenomic analysis further revealed that V(V) reduction genes were potentially associated with reductive metabolism and electron transfer genes. The microbiome in MiA exhibited the highest cytochrome c levels and the strongest expression of potential V(V) reduction genes, highlighting microorganisms derived from MiA-aggregates as primary drivers of vanadium detoxification in contaminated soils.

title: XAS evidence for Sb(V)-ferrihydrite reduction into Sb(III)-magnetite during anoxic incubation of stormwater road basin sediments
description: Publication date: Available online 1 August 2026 Source: Applied Geochemistry Author(s): Areej Adra, Maëva Philippe, Pierre Le Pape, Georges Ona-Nguema, Gautier Landrot, Ludovic Delbes, Elora Bourbon, Katell Quénéa, Sophie Ayrault
abstract: Antimony (Sb) presents versatile chemical forms in urban (sub)surface environments, the identity of which being driven by local redox conditions. Due to its use as additive in products for its flame-retardant properties, urban environments such as the Parisian area (Paris, France) are particularly subjected to Sb enrichment. This is particularly observed in stormwater basin sediments, collecting Sb from runoff on road surfaces. Here, we used these sediments as a reactive ecosystem for aging Sb-bearing ferrihydrite, standing as a classical Sb carrier phase of surface environments and as possible input phase to the basins. Batch experiments were performed by mixing stormwater pond sediments plus Sb(V)-bearing ferrihydrite (Fh-Sb(V)) and were aged up to 210 days under a water column in oxic or anoxic conditions. For each series, an individual batch sample was sampled at 1, 7, 28 and 210 days of aging. Liquid samples were analyzed by ICP-MS, while Fe and Sb speciation were studied by X-ray absorption spectroscopy (XANES/EXAFS) to study Sb release to surface waters and the temporal evolution of Sb speciation. Whatever the experimental conditions, Sb release into solution remains below one percent of the initial stock introduced in the sediment, decorrelated of Fe(II) release and organic matter consumption during reduction processes. Under anoxic conditions, XANES data at the Fe K-edge show the transformation of ferrihydrite into magnetite. From EXAFS analysis at the Sb K-edge, we unambiguously identify a novel reaction route, Sb(V)-bearing ferrihydrite reduction into Sb(III)-bearing magnetite, likely resulting from anoxic aging in a biotic medium. In the oxic experiment, diffusion of air through the initially anoxic water column resulted in the late oxidation of the newly Sb(III)-magnetite formed into Sb(V)-bearing phases. This study shows the strong geochemical reactivity of Sb when submitted to redox fluctuations and that iron-reducing activity likely drives Sb speciation in the presence of available Fe from poorly-crystalline ferrihydrite (Fh). Thus, the fundamental knowledge we bring here could help to define conditions propitious to limiting soluble Sb release from the solid phase in contaminated sediments submitted to redox fluctuations.

title: Human activities as primary drivers of marine and inland groundwater salinization in the Costa de Hermosillo aquifer system
description: Publication date: Available online 22 July 2026 Source: Applied Geochemistry Author(s): Christian Narvaez-Montoya, Saugata Datta, Jürgen Mahlknecht, Miguel Rangel-Medina
abstract: Groundwater salinization is a major threat to coastal aquifers worldwide, particularly in arid and semi-arid regions subjected to intensive groundwater use. Understanding the behavior of individual coastal aquifer systems is therefore essential to support effective groundwater management. This study evaluates the spatiotemporal salinization patterns of the Costa de Hermosillo aquifer system, located at the coastal margin of the Sonoran Desert, using 357 groundwater samples collected in 2009 and 2016, primarily from the most productive and shallow hydrogeological unit. Multivariate and hydrogeochemical analyses suggest that seawater intrusion is the dominant driver of total dissolved solids and chloride enrichment, strongly linked to long-term overexploitation. Inland, heterogeneous nitrate and sulfate distributions suggest the influence of anthropogenic inputs, including urban wastewater infiltration and irrigation return flow. Temporal comparisons indicate a decrease in nitrate concentrations, likely reflecting improved wastewater treatment, alongside a significant increase in sulfate, which may be associated with enhanced water-rock interaction processes previously linked to irrigation practices. 15% of samples exceed drinking water guideline limits, and 47% exhibit poor irrigation water quality, highlighting potential risks for human consumption, soil salinization, and agricultural productivity. This study provides one of the most comprehensive recent assessments of salinization processes in the Costa de Hermosillo aquifer system and emphasizes the need to reduce groundwater abstraction and strengthen wastewater and irrigation management to prevent further degradation of the aquifer. Because the interpretations are based on major ions and previous studies, future investigations incorporating more sensitive tracers are needed to better constrain the mechanisms responsible for groundwater salinization.

title: Source of Uranium (U) and Rare Earth Elements (REE) for Unconformity-Related U and REE Mineralization in the Athabasca Basin, Canada: Insights from Accessory Minerals in Sandstones
description: Publication date: Available online 25 June 2026 Source: Applied Geochemistry Author(s): Goktug Harmanci, Guoxiang Chi, Jeremy Powell, Janina Czas, Victoria Tschirhart, Huimin Su, Yumeng Wang, Nahanni Danylczuk
abstract: The Athabasca Basin in Canada hosts the world’s largest and highest-grade unconformity-related uranium (URU) deposits, many of which are also enriched in rare earth elements (REE). There has been a long-lasting debate whether the U and REE were sourced from the basin or basement. This study investigates the potential contribution of detrital accessory minerals in the basin, particularly zircon and Ti-oxide (rutile), to U and REE mineralization. The textural and compositional characteristics of these detrital accessory minerals, as well as diagenetic minerals, including Ti-oxide (anatase), iron oxide/hydroxide (IOH) and aluminium phosphate sulfate (APS) minerals, were examined using multiple in-situ analytical methods. The results show that detrital zircon and rutile exhibit extensive dissolution and alteration features and large and irregular variations of U and REE concentrations within individual grains suggesting strong fluid-rock interactions. Large amounts of U and REE, especially heavy REE (HREE), were leached into the basinal brines, while some of them, especially light REE (LREE), were retained by diagenetic minerals. The resulting diagenetic basinal fluids are characterized by strong HREE enrichment, which broadly match the REE patterns of uraninite in the URU ores. Mass balance calculations suggest that 40 to 70 million tonnes of U and 80 to 330 million tonnes of REE, depending on the methods of calculation, could be leached from zircon and rutile. Despite the large variations and uncertainties, these estimations far exceed the amounts found in the URU deposits, implying significant potentials for further U and REE exploration. The results also highlight the vulnerability of zircon and rutile to hydrothermal alteration under certain conditions in sedimentary basins and its significance for large-scale U and REE mineralization.

title: Ca isotope fractionation during precipitation of authigenic carbonates: A case study from the Haima cold seep, northern South China Sea
description: Publication date: 5 October 2026 Source: Chemical Geology, Volume 721 Author(s): Jingya Cao, Junming Zhou, Junxi Feng, Jun Tao, Jie Xuan, Shengxiong Yang
abstract: Calcium isotopes serve as a sensitive tracer for carbonate formation processes, yet the mechanisms governing Ca isotopic fractionation during authigenic carbonate precipitation, particularly in dynamic cold-seep systems, remain debated. This study presents integrated elemental (Sr/Ca and Mg/Ca) and isotopic (C-O-Sr-Ca) data from two types of authigenic carbonates (chimney and shell-bearing) recovered from the two sites with high methane flux in the Haima cold seep, northern South China Sea (SCS). The chimney carbonates exhibit strongly negative δ13CV-PDB values of −33.3‰ to −30.1‰ and positive δ18OV-PDB values of 3.62–4.31‰, whereas the shell-bearing carbonates exhibit δ13CV-PDB values of −45.2‰ to −42.1‰ and δ18OV-PDB values of 3.85–4.34‰, confirming their methane seepage-related carbon and oxygen origin. Most of the samples show elevated Sr/Ca and depleted Mg/Ca mass ratios, consistent with a predominantly aragonitic composition, though a minor subset is calcite-dominated. It is indicated that Sr/Ca and Mg/Ca ratios are mostly controlled by the carbonate mineralogy rather than the precipitation rate. The 87Sr/86Sr ratios (0.709178–0.709278) of these authigenic carbonates closely match modern seawater signatures, indicating that authigenic carbonate formed within high methane flux shows significant potential for preserving the 87Sr/86Sr signature of ancient seawater. Calcium isotope compositions (δ44/40Ca) range from 0.73‰ to 1.37‰ and show strong correlations with Mg/Ca (positive) and Sr/Ca (negative) ratios, suggesting that carbonate mineralogy exerts a primary control on Ca isotopic fractionation. These findings highlight the pivotal role of carbonate mineralogy in governing the Sr and Mg concentrations and Ca isotopic signatures of authigenic carbonates in cold seeps.

title: First oxygen isotopic data of coexisting glauconite and celadonite by NanoSIMS
description: Publication date: 5 October 2026 Source: Chemical Geology, Volume 721 Author(s): Elisa Laita, Maria Àngels Subirana, Dirk Schaumlöffel, Matías Reolid, Isabel Abad, Fernando Nieto, Blanca Bauluz
abstract: This study presents the first nanoscale secondary ion mass spectrometry (NanoSIMS) oxygen isotopic analyses in coexisting glauconite and celadonite related to hydrothermal alteration of Jurassic pillow-lavas from the Subbetic (Betic Cordillera, South Spain). The slight differences in Fe and K content of these two micas allowed them to be differentiated by focused ion beam scanning electron microscopy (FIB-SEM) and extract them as separate 10 × 5 μm size and 1 μm thick lamellae of each mineral. This sample preparation eliminated the need of preliminary elemental mapping by NanoSIMS to identify the different minerals within the sample before the isotopic mapping. However, the small thickness of the studied lamellae caused their fast consumption during oxygen isotopic mapping. Together with the H-isotope fractionation that micas can undergo during heating and dehydroxylation this could prevent the later acquisition of deuterium measurements. NanoSIMS reported an average 18O/16O ratio for glauconite of 2.05 × 10−3 (±1.14 × 10−5), whereas the average ratio for celadonite was 2.02 × 10−3 (±1.43 × 10−5). The δ18OSMOW values obtained separately for glauconite (29 ‰ ±6) and celadonite (18 ‰ ±6), despite the standard deviations, demonstrate that NanoSIMS could be applicable for analysing the oxygen isotopic composition of coexisting small-size clay minerals within the same sample. According to these preliminary results, the studied glauconite and celadonite could have a partial overlap in their formation conditions, with celadonite beginning to crystallise just as glauconite crystallisation finishes.

title: Noble gas constraints on open-system fluid evolution and selective gas loss in tight sandstone reservoirs of the Xinchang gas field, Sichuan Basin
description: Publication date: 5 October 2026 Source: Chemical Geology, Volume 721 Author(s): Jamie Robert Beagle, Shengfei Qin, Yunpeng Wang, Chengsheng Chen, Chunhui Cao, Greg Holland, Ben Surridge, Zheng Zhou
abstract: Understanding how noble gases record fluid sources, migration pathways and degrees of openness in complex tight sandstone reservoirs remains a key challenge in subsurface geochemistry. The Xinchang gas field in the Sichuan Basin hosts significant CH4-rich (89.43–97.36%) tight sandstone reservoirs within the Triassic Xujiahe Formation (T3 x), and the Jurassic Shaximiao (J2 s) and Qianfoya (J2 q) formations, providing an ideal setting to investigate these processes. Noble gas compositions (He, Ne, Ar, Kr and Xe) from 12 production wells were analysed to constrain the charging, accumulation and evolution of fluids within low porosity (<5%), ultra-low matrix permeability (<0.1 mD) reservoirs. Measured 3He/4He ratios (0.0037–0.025 Ra; Ra = atmospheric 3He/4He), indicate dominantly crustal radiogenic He with minor atmospheric contributions introduced through groundwater interaction. Strongly fractionated 20Ne/36Ar ratios relative to air-saturated water (ASW; <0.14), record open-system degassing and multistage Ne loss during migration. Atmospheric excesses in 21Ne and 40Ar further demonstrate prolonged gas-water exchange, and mixing between crustal fluids and groundwater, while elevated 4He/20Ne ratios reflect substantial accumulation of radiogenic 4He. Moderately enriched 40Ar/36Ar ratios (≤858.2) relative to air (298.56) similarly indicate mixing between atmospheric and crustal components. Noble gas systematics demonstrate that Xinchang tight sandstone reservoirs have not behaved as closed systems. Instead, fluid evolution reflects episodic gas-water exchange, degassing and structurally modified fluid connectivity that facilitated mixing between atmospheric, crustal and hydrocarbon-derived components and enabled partial gas loss from the system. These results highlight the value of noble gases as tracers of fluid evolution and permeability development in unconventional reservoir systems.

title: Early seawater-derived dolomite altered under distinct geochemical-buffering conditions: Insights into early diagenetic remobilization of rare earth elements
description: Publication date: 5 October 2026 Source: Chemical Geology, Volume 721 Author(s): Misbahu Abdullahi, Cathy Hollis, Adhipa Herlambang, Khalid Al-Ramadan, Massimo Tiepolo, Ardiansyah Koeshidayatullah
abstract: Early-formed seawater-derived dolomite is often used to reconstruct seawater chemistry and fluid-rock interaction, yet the fidelity of its geochemical proxies remains uncertain. Rare earth elements (REE) are commonly regarded as immobile during diagenesis. However, growing evidence suggests that REE can be remobilized even under low water-rock interactions. Here, we present petrographic, isotopic, and REE data from early-formed dolomite (RD1) of the Musayr Formation, northwest Saudi Arabia, to evaluate geochemical proxy preservation, inheritance, and remobilization during early diagenesis. The host limestone shows evidence of pervasive meteoric alteration, pre-dating dolomitization, and exhibits a near-flat to MREE-bulged pattern, consistent with diagenetic remobilization of REE. The analyzed Oyster shells display vitally fractionated trace and REE signatures but meteorically modified δ13C–δ18O values, questioning the reliability of their isotopic fingerprints for paleo-seawater reconstructions. Two distinct RD1 dolomite types are defined. The first (RD1-TUs) has δ13C, δ18O, REE patterns, and Y/Ho ratios indicative of formation from near-normal seawater under suboxic, restricted conditions, with indication of strong rock buffering of REE. The second type (RD1-2MWB) exhibits an MREE-bulged pattern and elevated Fe–Mn–Sr concentrations, reflecting localized recrystallization under more reducing conditions or analytical contamination artifact. This suggests that REE deviations reflect coupled remobilization within host carbonates and marine restriction during RD1-TUs dolomitization, rather than open-system diagenesis. These findings demonstrate that early seawater-derived dolomite can retain marine isotopic signatures while recording non-seawater REE patterns governed by rock-buffered diagenesis. Crucially, different geochemical proxies capture distinct diagenetic processes, underscoring the need for multi-proxy approaches in paleoenvironmental reconstructions.

title: Deciphering environmental processes in sedimentary carbonates, a dynamic isotope box model approach
description: Publication date: 5 October 2026 Source: Chemical Geology, Volume 721 Author(s): Robin Havas, Christophe Thomazo, Rosaluz Tavera, Vladimir Betancourt, Élodie Muller, Jeanne Caumartin, Didier Jézéquel, Karim Benzerara
abstract: Carbon and oxygen isotope records of sedimentary carbonates (δ13Ccarb and δ18Ocarb) are among the most widely used proxies for paleoenvironmental reconstructions, although their interpretation can be complicated by complex and overprinting processes. Here we present an innovative dynamic box model to unravel the environmental implications of δ13Ccarb and δ18Ocarb, that we apply and constrain in a modern lacustrine setting. We compare the simulated isotopic trends with those measured in the lake sedimentary carbonates over the last 60 years and confront our modeled dissolved inorganic carbon concentrations in the lake with reported measurements for the same period. While most of the relevant environmental parameters of the studied volcanic Lake Alchichica (Mexico) are well constrained, tuning the remaining inputs of the model allows a quantitative assessment of the environmental processes governing the lake's hydrological, carbon and oxygen cycles. Most notably, our results reveal that a clear imbalance in the lake's C budget and δ13C data can only be resolved if the model includes a substantial – but previously unrecognized – volcanic CO2 degassing flux to the lake. Our results further support that groundwater extraction and agriculture in the area have increasingly affected the lake's hydrological and C balance since the 1980s. Overall, we show that this alkaline lake, despite high biological productivity and massive carbonate deposition, is a net CO2 source to the atmosphere. Through a thorough parametrization and characterization of the C and O fluxes in a modern setting, this new modeling approach hold promises for reconstructing ancient environments from carbonate isotope archives.

title: Contrasting Fe(II)-catalyzed phase transformation of biogenic and abiogenic ferrihydrite
description: Publication date: 5 October 2026 Source: Chemical Geology, Volume 721 Author(s): Weifu Wang, Qunwei Dai, Xiaobo Luo, Jun Guo, Yuanjie Xie, Weiqi Du, Wenmei Peng, Min Wei, Zhijing Zhang, Yunbi Huang
abstract: The transformation of ferrihydrite plays a key role in controlling the mobility and transformation of contaminants in the environment. In Fe2+-rich environments, iron-oxidizing microorganisms (e.g., Crenothrix, Leptothrix, and Gallionella) can produce abundant sheaths and stalks composed of ferrihydrite and organic components, forming typical biogenic ferrihydrite (Bio-Fh). However, whether organic components associated with Bio-Fh result in distinct transformation behaviors compared with abiotic ferrihydrite remains unclear. In this study, the Fe(II)-catalyzed phase transformation of Abio-Fh and Bio-Fh was systematically compared by investigating transformation products, organic components, Fe2+ consumption, as well as changes in microstructure and porosity. The results show that Abio-Fh completely transforms into goethite and magnetite with increasing Fe2+ concentrations. In contrast, Bio-Fh exhibits limited transformation, reaching a maximum transformation extent of ∼40% at both 2 and 4 mM Fe2+, with lepidocrocite and goethite as the products. The transformation of Abio-Fh induces substantial structural and morphological reconstruction, whereas Bio-Fh experiences partial reconstruction while retaining its original structural characteristics. These differences are primarily attributed to the interaction between organic matter and ferrihydrite, which limits the efficiency of Fe(II)-mineral electron transfer and suppresses subsequent structural rearrangement, thereby inhibiting the phase transformation process. The organic matter in Bio-Fh can be further classified into weakly bound, moderately bound, and strongly bound. The weakly and moderately bound fractions are the major components involved in regulating ferrihydrite transformation. These differences may alter the environmental fate of elements and contaminants by modifying the stability and reactivity of ferrihydrite.

title: Tracing provenance and diagenetic history of Mesoproterozoic organic-rich shales from the McArthur Basin, Australia, using coupled Rb-Sr and K-Ar illite dating
description: Publication date: 5 October 2026 Source: Chemical Geology, Volume 721 Author(s): Yaser Noorian, Juraj Farkaš, Alan S. Collins, Claudio Delle Piane, Andrew Todd, Sarah E. Gilbert, Rong Fan, Cecilia Loyola
abstract: Authigenic to early diagenetic clay minerals, particularly illite, are abundant in Proterozoic basins and fine-grained sedimentary rocks, preserving records of depositional, early diagenetic and post-depositional processes. However, distinguishing the primary depositional elemental and isotopic signatures from the later diagenetic overprints in ancient sedimentary archives remains challenging, particularly in Proterozoic systems. This complexity is illustrated on the studied organic-rich shales of the Velkerri Formation, deposited at ca. 1430 to 1360 Ma in the McArthur Basin, Australia, where the timing of clay authigenesis and/or later stage diagenetic resetting remains poorly constrained. Here, we investigate illite–smectite clay mineral separates from the Velkerri Formation shales, which preserve a complex isotopic and geochronological record reflecting both older detrital provenance sources and younger or post-depositional diagenetic overprints. Acquired in-situ Rb-Sr and ‘bulk’ K-Ar dating of grain-size–separated clay fractions reveal systematic age differences between coarser, detrital-rich fractions and finer, illite-dominated fractions. The coarser fractions (0.2–2 μm) yielded older or Mesoproterozoic Rb-Sr ages (∼1050–1340 Ma), which thus post-date the expected depositional ages, while the fine fractions (<0.2 μm) record predominantly younger and variably reset ages, spanning from 760 to 1135 Ma for Rb-Sr and 860 to 970 Ma for K-Ar systems. These younger or Neoproterozoic ages thus reflect isotopic resetting associated with later-stage fluid-driven or tectono-thermal alteration of the studied shales. A simple detrital vs. authigenic ‘end-member’ mixing model constrains the timing of such younger alteration event(s) to ca. 805–850 Ma, coincident with the Tonian tectono-thermal activity related to Rodinia rifting and breakup and the initiation of the Centralian Superbasin. Complementary REE data collected from the studied shales/clay separates support this interpretation, with LREE and MREE depletion observed in the fine-grained authigenic clays indicating fluid–rock interaction linked to such younger or late-stage illitization, rather than detrital REE sources. Collectively, these results demonstrate that clay-hosted REE patterns and coupled Rb-Sr and K-Ar geochronometers are sensitive indicators of a multiphase post-depositional shale alteration, capturing both inherited provenance ages and also younger Neoproterozoic diagenetic resetting, thus providing new constraints on the timing of Tonian tectonic or fluid-flow alteration event(s) impacting the McArthur Basin and its sedimentary records.

title: Divergent temperature responses of organo-mineral fractions across alpine wetlands
description: Publication date: 5 October 2026 Source: Chemical Geology, Volume 721 Author(s): Bin Niu, Xiang Chen, Xiaoqin Yang, Ya Yang, Huiyuan Wang, Hongzhe Jiao, Tianzhu Lei, Dashuan Tian, Gengxin Zhang
abstract: Alpine wetlands represent one of the most important terrestrial organic carbon (OC) sinks, owing to their low temperatures, high soil moisture, and unique hydrological regimes. These ecosystems store large quantities of soil organic carbon (SOC) not only in particulate organic matter (POM) but also in mineral-associated organic matter (MAOM), which is generally considered more stable due to organo-mineral interactions. According to the mineral stabilization mechanism, MAOM can be further partitioned into distinct organo-mineral fractions, which may differ in their stability and temperature sensitivity under climate warming. Here, by applying sequential chemical extractions along an altitudinal gradient of Tibetan alpine wetlands, we fractionated SOC into six components and identified two functionally distinct MAOM clusters. The metal-bound cluster (9.8–36.1% of SOC), including weakly adsorbed organic matter and metal-OM complexes, showed increasing abundance with rising temperature. In contrast, the mineral-bound cluster (59.2–75.0% of SOC), including short-range ordered (SRO) Fe/Al-OM, carbonate-associated OM, Fe oxyhydroxide-OM, and residual OM, exhibited no significant temperature dependence. This divergence reflects contrasting stabilization pathways: the metal-bound cluster is largely governed by biologically mediated processes and Ca-bridging interactions that are sensitive to temperature, whereas the mineral-bound cluster is primarily regulated by geochemical weathering and the stabilization capacity of Fe/Al oxides, which are less responsive to short-term thermal shifts. Our findings demonstrate that different organo-mineral fractions within MAOM exhibit divergent responses to warming, suggesting that alpine wetland soils cannot be treated as a homogeneous carbon pool in climate‑carbon feedback models. These results highlight the critical importance of considering stabilization mechanisms and fraction-specific dynamics when predicting soil carbon persistence and vulnerability in alpine wetlands under ongoing climate change.

title: Mercury isotopes trace (meta-)sedimentary melting in pegmatite lithium mineralization in the Eastern Songpan-Ganzi Belt, China
description: Publication date: 5 October 2026 Source: Chemical Geology, Volume 721 Author(s): Weipeng Liu, Hui Zhang, Yong Tang, Zhenghang Lv, Shukuan Wu, Wei Mao, Changzhou Deng
abstract: Lithium-rich pegmatites represent a critical source of lithium, yet the roles of source nature in the large-scale lithium enrichment during their petrogenesis remain unclear. Mercury (Hg) isotopes, with their multidimensional tracing capability, offer unique advantages in identifying source characteristics and revealing the processes of exceptional elemental enrichment. In this study, we analyzed the Hg isotope compositions of ore-related S-type two-mica granites and their derived pegmatites, as well as regional unmineralized I-type quartz diorites and metasedimentary rocks from the eastern Songpan-Ganzi lithium belt, to constrain the nature of their source. Our study reveals that the two-mica granites and their associated pegmatites, both Li-mineralized and barren, display consistently negative δ202Hg (−0.64 ± 0.49‰, 1SD, n = 34) and Δ199Hg (−0.09 ± 0.07‰, 1SD, n = 34) values. These Hg isotopic fingerprints closely match those of the regional Xikang and Bayan Har metasedimentary rocks (δ202Hg: −1.19 ± 0.69‰; Δ199Hg: −0.08 ± 0.12‰, 1SD, n = 10) and global terrestrial sediments, indicating a continental (meta-)sedimentary source for the parental magma. In contrast, the quartz diorite displays negative δ202Hg values (−0.86 ± 0.39‰, 1SD, n = 6) but near-zero Δ199Hg values (0.02 ± 0.05‰, 1SD, n = 6), indicating negligible recycling of Hg in its magma source, which is inferred to be mantle-derived juvenile crustal components. Based on these observations, we propose that post-orogenic crustal thinning triggered partial melting of (meta-)sedimentary sequences, facilitating the initial enrichment of the highly incompatible element Li. Consequently, we infer that the widespread formation of pegmatite-type lithium deposits was predominantly governed by large-scale melting of continental (meta-)sedimentary sequences.

title: Punctuated garnet growth within a protracted zircon record distinguishes reaction dates from residence times in North Qaidam eclogites
description: Publication date: 30 September 2026 Source: Chemical Geology, Volume 720 Author(s): Kai-Yang Du, Hao Cheng, Ruyi Yang
abstract: Constraining the duration of (ultra)high-pressure metamorphism is central to quantifying rates of continental subduction and exhumation, yet the answer depends on which mineral is dated. Zircon U-Pb date spectra are routinely read as residence times, but zircon may grow, dissolve, and recrystallize across many stages of a pressure–temperature path, whereas garnet records the discrete reactions that produced it. We combine microsampled garnet Lu-Hf and Sm-Nd geochronology, zircon U-Pb dating, trace-element systematics, phase-equilibrium modeling, and a quantitative modal rare-earth-element (REE) budget for eclogites from the Dulan area of the North Qaidam terrane. Garnet core and rim fractions from three samples yield indistinguishable Lu-Hf dates ranging from 439.1 ± 1.8 to 442.5 ± 1.9 Ma, recording garnet growth within analytical resolution at ∼2.6–3.0 GPa and 660–720 °C. Pseudosection modeling links this garnet growth to a single overstepped dehydration reaction releasing ∼1.6 wt% water. Zircon dates, by contrast, span ca. 484–427 Ma, and zircon trace-element and Ti-in-zircon systematics evolve systematically through this interval, indicating growth and modification across multiple stages rather than continuous eclogite-facies residence. Modal REE budget calculations show that flat heavy-REE patterns are non-unique, as retrograde amphibole and epidote or zoisite can reproduce an eclogite-like signature. These results demonstrate that garnet and zircon monitor fundamentally distinct processes: a discrete reaction pulse versus an integrated history. Their divergence, not their agreement, is diagnostic of metamorphic evolution. Comparison with other large (U)HP terranes shows that apparent multi-million-year “protracted” (U)HP spectra can readily emerge from short, single-rock garnet pulses combined with diachronous burial and exhumation of tectonic slices. Accessory-mineral-only chronologies may therefore conflate distinct reactions with prolonged residence. Mineral dates in (U)HP terranes must first be read as reaction dates, using growth-pulse geochronology, zircon compositional and thermometric trends, and modal REE budgets, before they can be converted into residence-time estimates.

title: Rare earth element exchange during seafloor weathering and its role in the Nd isotopic composition of paleo-seawater
description: Publication date: 30 September 2026 Source: Chemical Geology, Volume 720 Author(s): L.A. Coogan, K.M. Gillis, J. Spence
abstract: Rare earth elements are generally considered immobile during seafloor weathering (i.e., low temperature alteration of seafloor basalts) and this has led to the role of seafloor weathering in controlling the Nd isotopic composition of seawater being neglected. However, during times when deep ocean waters were warmer, seafloor weathering was much more extensive than it is in the modern ocean, which increases the potential for seafloor weathering to have contributed to the Nd isotopic composition of the ancient ocean. Without understanding the role of seafloor weathering in the ocean Nd cycle, paleo-oceanographic reconstructions for times when bottom water was warmer (e.g., the Paleocene and Cretaceous), may be subject to systematic errors. We present chemical data demonstrating large scale REE mobility in the upper ∼100 m of the lavas of the Cretaceous age Troodos ophiolite (Cyprus). Relative to the fresh lavas, these have large negative Ce anomalies and lower εNd. These REE mobility proxies correlate with one another and trend towards the composition of Neotethys seawater. Correlated Ce anomalies and εNd can be quantitatively explained by reactive transport models with large seawater fluxes. Neodymium concentrations in altered and fresh lavas are similar suggesting isotope exchange is decoupled from elemental fluxes. The trace element compositions of void filling calcite formed during seafloor weathering support this suggestion. These observations require the average partition coefficient for Nd between the altered lavas and seawater-derived fluids to be similar to the concentration ratio between fresh basalt and seawater. This may be fortuitous or may indicate that seawater REE concentrations are buffered by reactions with altered seafloor basalts or similar rocks. Overall, we conclude Nd isotope exchange during seafloor weathering should be considered when interpreting paleo-oceanographic Nd isotope proxies for times when bottom water temperatures were high.

title: In-situ Rb Sr dating of the crystalline basement beneath the Amadeus Basin, Australia: Implications for the radiogenic helium generation, migration and extreme 4 He accumulation
description: Publication date: 30 September 2026 Source: Chemical Geology, Volume 720 Author(s): Cecilia Loyola, Juraj Farkaš, Alan S. Collins, Jason Alexander Charlwood, Sarah E. Gilbert, Peter W. Haines
abstract: The crystalline basement beneath the Amadeus Basin (central Australia) hosts one of the world's highest recorded helium (He) concentrations (up to 9%) together with significant hydrogen (∼11%). The radiogenic 4He accumulated in the Neoproterozoic sedimentary succession of the Amadeus Basin was generated by alpha decay of U and Th in minerals of the underlying Proterozoic granitic basement. Initially retained within mineral lattices, He was later released through microfracturing. Constraining the timing of basement formation and subsequent fracturing is therefore critical to quantify long-term 4He production and migration. We applied in-situ RbSr dating using LA-ICP-MS/MS to primary K-rich igneous minerals (orthoclase, muscovite) and to secondary fine-grained micas and sericite hosted in microfractures from granitic basement beneath the Amadeus Basin, recovered from >2 km depth via the Jacko Bore 1 drillhole. Primary minerals yielded an age of 1100 ± 30 Ma, consistent with the timing of cooling following the Musgrave Orogeny. Secondary micas and sericite produced younger ages (642 ± 31 Ma to 517 ± 22 Ma), corresponding to deformation during the Ediacaran–Cambrian Petermann Orogeny. The concentrations of U and Th in basement rocks were determined by LA-ICP-MS and combined with Nuclear Emulsion Gel imaging to identify alpha-emitting and 4He producing domains. Integration of geochronology and trace element data enabled modelling of radiogenic 4He production from the Proterozoic to present. Modelled He isotope compositions agree with published 3He/4He ratios (0.031 Ra) from Jacko Bore 1 gas samples, demonstrating the utility of in-situ RbSr geochronology for evaluating radiogenic helium system.

title: Desert flashfloods recorded by Ba/Ca in benthic marine foraminifera ( Operculina ammonoides )
description: Publication date: 30 September 2026 Source: Chemical Geology, Volume 720 Author(s): Beverly Goodman-Tchernov, Shai Oron, Aleksey Sadekov, Gilad Antler, Timor Katz
abstract: River discharge proxies are essential for reconstructing terrestrial precipitation patterns and long-term climatic variability. Unfortunately, easily distinguishable direct proxies such as the presence of terrestrial muds in the sea are often missing after being winnowed and removed from the near-shore stratigraphy, or altered due to mixing and bioturbation. Barium, which is abundant in terrestrial sediments, is delivered to the sea via these runoff events in dissolved and particulate forms. Barium-to‑calcium (Ba/Ca) ratios in carbonate skeletons of marine organisms have proven to be an indicator of discharge events, though their application in benthic foraminifera remains under-studied. In particular, their capacity to resolve individual events in perennial systems where seasonal contrasts are often muted has not been explored. This study investigates Ba/Ca ratios in live benthic foraminifera (Operculina ammonoides) from the shallow marine shelf of the hyper-arid Gulf of Aqaba–Eilat. This setting provides a unique natural laboratory where ephemeral river (wadi) floods are rare and brief, potentially providing an isolated geochemical runoff signal. Our results demonstrate that foraminiferal chambers precipitated within five months of a flood event exhibit Ba/Ca ratios approximately double the background levels (∼8 versus ∼4 μmol/mol). Stable Mg/Ca ratios and historical water parameters negate temperature and pH as drivers of this enrichment. These findings suggest that Ba/Ca ratios in shallow-shelf benthic foraminifera are controlled by post-flood changes in the porewater, thereby successfully archiving desert flash floods. Consequently, and with added calibration this may provide a potent proxy for reconstructing high-resolution paleohydrology in arid coastal regions and offers a potential framework for developing paleo-environmental proxies in coastal settings generally.

title: The role of water in the generation of I-type barren granitic pegmatites
description: Publication date: 30 September 2026 Source: Chemical Geology, Volume 720 Author(s): L.M. Fonseca Teixeira, M. Ackerson, O. Bachmann
abstract: Surging demand for critical elements highlights the need to understand how they concentrate in Earth's crust. Granitic pegmatites are key hosts of many rare metals, yet most pegmatites are unmineralized, prompting the question of what controls their fertility. Here, we challenge the traditional view of pegmatites as “residual granites” and propose that barren pegmatites share thermal histories with granitic parents. Using global geochemical datasets, we suggest that prior enrichment of the melt is unlikely to drive mineralization. Thermodynamic models and mineral chemistry from the I-type Bergell intrusion (Switzerland) show that silicic melts with high initial water content (i.e. H₂O > 6–8 wt% at the liquidus) trigger early fluid exsolution, forming chemically unfractionated pegmatites. Our Bergell data provide proof of concept, revealing pegmatites and granites with coeval cold crystallization at near and below the water-saturated haplogranitic solidus temperatures. We suggest that I-type granites are typically cold, wet, and ultimately host barren pegmatites, while drier S- and A-type granites host more mineralized pegmatites.

title: Citric acid redirects abiotic Mn(II) oxidation toward poorly crystalline hexagonal birnessite-like phases under circumneutral conditions
description: Publication date: 30 September 2026 Source: Chemical Geology, Volume 720 Author(s): Feng Zhang, Yanting Pan, Shuai Lan, Xiaoming Wang, Hui Yin, Zimeng Wang, Wenfeng Tan, Xionghan Feng
abstract: Abiotic oxidation of dissolved Mn(II) by O2 under circumneutral conditions commonly yields low-valence Mn oxides, whereas Mn(IV)-rich hexagonal birnessite is more often associated with microbial Mn(II) oxidation. Here we show that citric acid (CA) substantially alters this abiotic pathway by stabilizing filter-passing oxidized Mn species and redirecting mineral formation toward poorly crystalline hexagonal birnessite-like phase. Time-resolved kinetic experiments show that CA eliminates the initial lag phase and accelerates early accumulation of filter-passing oxidized Mn, but suppresses the later autocatalytic oxidation on Mn oxide surfaces. The reaction therefore evolves through three concentration-dependent stages: rapid accumulation of soluble/colloidal oxidized Mn, a plateau marked by dynamic balance between oxidation and decomposition of oxidized intermediates, and a later stage of inhibited heterogeneous Mn(II) oxidation and precipitation. Spectroscopic and microscopic analyses show that, in the absence of CA, oxidation produces a well-crystalline assemblage dominated by feitknechtite and triclinic birnessite, whereas low to moderate CA concentrations favor poorly crystalline hexagonal birnessite-like products and higher Mn average oxidation states. At higher CA concentrations, this trend weakens and lower-valence phases such as bixbyite and rhodochrosite become more abundant. These observations are consistent with a pathway in which CA stabilizes filter-passing oxidized Mn species, likely including Mn(III)-ligand species and colloidal Mn oxides, thereby redirecting precipitation toward hexagonal birnessite-like products. These results identify a ligand-mediated abiotic pathway by which organic complexation can control Mn redox kinetics, oxidized Mn mobility, and birnessite-like polytype selection under circumneutral conditions.

title: Evolution of reactive Fe minerals in paddy soils: constraints from Fe isotopes and spectroscopy
description: Publication date: 30 September 2026 Source: Chemical Geology, Volume 720 Author(s): Zhao Wang, Xiaodong Song, Huayong Wu, Zhen Zeng, Wei Li, Ganlin Zhang
abstract: Reactive Fe minerals are highly dynamic phases that play a critical role in regulating elemental cycling in soils, yet their formation and transformation under sustained redox oscillations in field settings remain poorly constrained. Here we investigate the evolution of reactive Fe oxides along a paddy soil chronosequence developed on Quaternary red clays by combining Fe stable isotope analysis, chemical extractions, EXAFS and 57Fe Mössbauer spectroscopy. Spectroscopic characterizations and extractions show that paddy cultivation redistributes Fe from crystalline Fe oxides into reactive Fe phases, increasing the reactive Fe fraction in both short- and long-term paddy surface horizons and in deep horizons of the long-term paddy profile. Across the long-term profile, bulk soils are systematically heavier than porewaters, yielding positive Δ56Fesolid–porewater offsets (0.45–0.98‰). These offsets are integrated contrasts between post-cycle solid Fe and mobile Fe under natural flood–drain cycling and are consistent with cumulative Fe mobilization and formation of reactive Fe phases. Operationally-defined porewater isotopes further suggest depth-dependent differences in Fe cycling, with potentially stronger colloid−/ligand-associated influence near the surface and relatively greater importance of aqueous Fe at depth. Comparison with published soil datasets shows an exploratory inverse correlation between Δ56Fesolid–porewater and reactive Fe abundance across systems. These results demonstrate that Fe isotope systematics, especially coupled with spectroscopic and extraction-based approaches, may provide a useful tracer of reactive Fe evolution in redox-dynamic soils.

title: Tellurium in volcanic and sedimentary systems – from outgassing to sequestration
description: Publication date: 30 September 2026 Source: Chemical Geology, Volume 720 Author(s): N.B. Baumann, M. Regelous, T. Adatte, R.L. Rudnick, K. Chen, B. Schoene, G. Keller, N. Sharma, K.M. Haase
abstract: We describe a method for rapid and precise analysis of Te in geological materials using a conventional single-quadrupole ICP-MS coupled with a commercially available desolvating nebulizer. Unlike previous methods, this method allows analyses of other trace elements in the same sample solutions. A single step ion-exchange preconcentration extends the method to samples containing less than 0.5 ng/g of Te. Combining this method with new S-Cd-In-Tl data, we derive an updated estimate of the average Te concentration of the upper continental crust of 36.7 ± 1.6 ng/g based on the analyses of glacial diamictite composites. Analyses of basaltic lavas from the Deccan continental flood basalt province indicate that Te was not fractionated into sulfides but is largely degassed from lavas. This is supported by the high Te content of paleosol horizons interbedded with basaltic lava flows. Leaching experiments carried out on Early Eocene ashes and interbedded sediments, deposited during flood basalt volcanism in the North Atlantic, indicate that volcanic Te is tightly bound to the sediment matrix and silicate particulates and not readily mobilized after deposition. Our results confirm that Te concentrations in sedimentary rocks may be a useful proxy for past volcanism.

title: Dual-isotopic (δ 34 S and δ 18 O) evidence for net CO 2 release from the northwestern Himalayan catchments
description: Publication date: 30 September 2026 Source: Chemical Geology, Volume 720 Author(s): Rakesh Kumar Rout, Gyana Ranjan Tripathy, Satyabrata Das, Achyuth Venugopal, Nitish Kumar, Santosh Kumar Rai, Abhayanand Singh Maurya
abstract: The plausible linkage between Himalaya weathering and Cenozoic cooling often overlooks the CO2 release during sulfide oxidation (S-oxidation), which (unlike silicate weathering) has a positive climatic effect. In this study, dissolved sulfur (δ34SSO4) and oxygen (δ18OSO4) isotopic compositions for the Indus headwater basin have been investigated to evaluate the spatial distribution and rate of S-oxidation within the basin. The δ34SSO4 of these samples varies between −11 and 5‰ (n = 50), with lower values being observed for the mainstream samples (−4 ± 2‰; n = 12). Inverse modelling of major ions and δ34SSO4 data estimates the fraction of silicate-derived cations (0.12 ± 0.09) and sulfide-derived sulfates (f pyr ; 0.68 ± 0.28). The fraction of molecular O2 (f O2 ) involved in oxidation exhibits a negative correlation with the δ18OSO4/δ18OH2O ratio for a given f pyr value. Calculations involving δ18OSO4 and f pyr values show significant f O2 variations (<0.83), with higher values being observed for carbonate-dominated sub-basins. The CO2 uptake (1.4 × 105 mol/km2/yr) and release (4.4 × 105 mol/km2/yr) rates for the basin exceed the global riverine averages, and indicate a net CO2 release from the basin. The silicate weathering in the basin is mainly controlled by temperature, whereas intense S-oxidation is consistent with the basin lithology and extensive glacial cover. Modelling of present and compiled datasets for the entire basin confirms net CO2 release from the upper Indus basin and CO2 consumption in the floodplain regions. This underscores the dominant role of mountain erosion in driving pyrite oxidation in river basins, and hence, in the global carbon cycle.

title: Iron migration and isotope fractionation during estuarine sedimentary processes: Responses to monsoon intensity and climate events
description: Publication date: 30 September 2026 Source: Chemical Geology, Volume 720 Author(s): Jiarong Liu, Jinlong Ma, Guanhong Zhu, Kai Luo, Feng Ye, Fang Luo, Gangjian Wei
abstract: Iron (Fe) isotopes serve as a sensitive tracer of Fe biogeochemical cycles. However, their fractionation mechanisms during sedimentation and responses to the paleoenvironment remain inadequately constrained. Here, we analyze the Fe concentrations and isotopic compositions (δ56Fe) in bulk sediments and chemical extracts of a ∼ 2000-year-old sediment core from the Pearl River Estuary. Bulk sediments exhibit δ56Fe values (0.10–0.26‰) similar to those of riverine particulates, but with higher Fe/Al ratios. This indicates substantial Fe transformation during the sedimentary processes, which is not recorded by bulk δ56Fe values. Sequential extraction reveals that Fe (hydro) oxides (60.7–70.5% of total Fe) carry low δ56Fe values (0.06–0.17‰), and there is a positive correlation between δ56Fe and Fe/Mn, indicating the preferential incorporation of heavy isotopes during oxidation. The residue phase (19.9–30.0%) exhibits higher δ56Fe values (0.32–0.48‰), and a negative correlation between δ56Fe and chlorite suggests the preferential release of light isotopes during weathering. The organic phase is a minor Fe host (5.28–8.94%) with the lowest δ56Fe values (−0.20‰ to 0.02‰), indicating the preferential complexation of light Fe isotopes. Interestingly, the δ56Fe values of both the Fe (hydro) oxides and the residue phases respond to climatic events (e.g., Late Antique Little Ice Age, Medieval Warm Period, and Little Ice Age). Furthermore, the δ56Fe values of the Fe (hydro) oxides record redox conditions driven by climate change. The δ56Fe values of the residue phase exhibit consistent variation with the East Asian Winter Monsoon intensity proxy (foraminifera δ18O), indicating that the Fe isotopic compositions may record the monsoon intensity. Bulk δ56Fe integrates signals from multiple Fe pools, obscuring direct climatic interpretation. Therefore, the analysis of individual phases is necessary to provide new insights for reconstructing monsoon intensity and paleoclimate.

title: Local structure of trace elements in basaltic glass up to Earth's lower mantle pressures with implications for melt densification and element partitioning
description: Publication date: 30 September 2026 Source: Chemical Geology, Volume 720 Author(s): Georgii Kovalskii, Angelika D. Rosa, Olivier Mathon, Wolfgang Morgenroth, Guillaume Morard, Lea Pennacchioni, João Elias Figueiredo Soares Rodrigues, Max Wilke
abstract: This study investigates pressure-induced local structural changes of strontium (Sr2+) and yttrium (Y3+) in basaltic silicate glasses up to 130 GPa. To monitor local structural changes of these minor elements we conducted X-ray absorption spectroscopy (XAS) experiments combined with the diamond anvil cell technique at room temperature. Both elements exhibit a two-stage reorganization of the local structure: in the first stage (up to ∼20 GPa), the average cation‑oxygen distance and cation's coordination number increase (for Sr from 6 to 8, for Y from 6 to 7); in the second stage, above 20–30 GPa, a progressive shortening of cation‑oxygen distance is observed, associated to the compression of coordination polyhedra. The two-stage compression scheme differs from that of network-forming cations, such as Si and Al. Those change from a corner-shared tetrahedral network to the closer packing of edge-sharing octahedra starting at 20–30 GPa. Due to the similarity of structural changes of Sr and Y to those around Ca and Mg, we conclude that their behavior reflects a universal trend for large cations in silicate melts during compression to conditions of the lower mantle. We used bond valence theory to validate the pressure-evolution of cation‑oxygen distances and compared them with data of crystalline counterparts. We expanded the bond valence theory by adding an additional pressure correction to ensure applicability at extreme pressure. The presented data improve our knowledge on local structural changes in basaltic melts across Earth's mantle pressures. We qualitatively assess the consequences for element partitioning between minerals and melt under core-mantle boundary conditions.

title: Titanium isotope fractionation in hydrous and oxidized large igneous provinces
description: Publication date: 30 September 2026 Source: Chemical Geology, Volume 720 Author(s): Sheng-Zhu Zhu, Xiao-Long Huang, Peng-Li He, Fan Yang, Jin-Long Ma, Yang Yu, Xin-Yue He, Le Zhang, Gang-Jian Wei
abstract: Titanium (Ti) isotopes have been utilized as tracers to determine the affinity of felsic rocks with either plumes or arcs, given that greater Ti isotope fractionation occurs in plume-related magmatism. However, it is essential to investigate whether this conclusion is universally applicable in hydrous and oxidized large igneous provinces (LIPs), as previous studies have primarily focused on water-poor and reduced plume-related rocks. This study presents the Ti isotope compositions of whole-rock samples and mineral separates from early Permian ultramafic–mafic–felsic rocks in the Wajilitag area of the hydrous and oxidized Tarim LIP (TLIP). The Wajilitag igneous rocks display Ti isotope fractionation (δ49Ti = −0.332‰ to +0.803‰), which is more pronounced than that in arc-related rocks, yet less significant compared to other plume-related rocks. Clinopyroxene, hornblende, biotite, and feldspar are slightly enriched in heavier Ti isotopes compared with their host rocks, whereas ilmenite and titanite are enriched in lighter Ti isotopes. Magnetite exhibits a wide range of Ti isotope compositions (δ49Ti = −0.120‰ to +2.247‰), with δ49Ti values increasing as TiO2 content decreases, heavier than equilibrium ilmenite. The mineral Ti isotopes indicate that primary magma TiO2, water contents (H2O), and oxygen fugacities (fO2) were the main factors controlling Ti isotope fractionation during magmatism. The primary magma of the TLIP has high TiO2 contents, as well as high H2O and fO2, which account for its medium Ti isotope fractionation between arc and plume magmatism. The interaction between plumes and subducted slab materials in the upper mantle is a key mechanism for the formation of hydrous and oxidized LIPs, resulting in deviations in Ti isotopes from typical plume magmas.

title: Heavy sulfur isotope of arc ultramafic cumulates revealed by S-rich apatite from the Dongwanzi intrusion, North China
description: Publication date: 30 September 2026 Source: Chemical Geology, Volume 720 Author(s): Huan Jennifer Chang, Mei-Fu Zhou, Wen-Jun Hu, Shengbiao Yang, Jian-Feng Gao
abstract: Arc magmas generally have higher sulfur (S) contents and higher δ34S values than mid-ocean ridge basalts. However, it remains debated whether the enrichment of S is due to crustal processes or mantle metasomatism. We present elemental and S-Sr isotopic compositions of apatite from the Early Permian Dongwanzi ultramafic intrusion, northern margin of the North China Craton. This arc intrusion is composed of clinopyroxenite and hornblendite based on textural relationships. Clinopyroxenites contains interstitial apatite and euhedral cumulus apatite. Interstitial apatite grains have high Cl (0.36–1.10 wt%), and Th (16.1–130 ppm), and La/Yb ratios (52.1–112), high 87Sr/86Sr ratios (0.70370–0.70391), and low δ34SV-CDT values (−10.5 to +4.44 ‰), consistent with crystallization from late-stage trapped melts. In contrast, euhedral cumulus apatite grains have low Cl (0.23–0.71 wt%), high δ34SV-CDT values (∼ + 7.9 ‰), and La/Yb ratios (33.4–64.6), and low initial 87Sr/86Sr ratios (∼0.70337), indicative of growth from a relatively primitive magma. Compared to cumulus apatite in clinopyroxenites, cumulus apatite grains in hornblendites contain high F (1.45–2.69 wt%) and total REE + Y (1510–9830 ppm), and high 87Sr/86Sr ratios (0.70333–0.70351), but slightly low Cl (0.01–0.50 wt%) and δ34SV-CDT (7.06 ‰ to 8.25 ‰), which were attributed to progressive fractional crystallization coupled with limited wall-rock contamination from clinopyroxenite to hornblendite. As a result, the consistently high δ34S values of cumulus apatite indicate that crustal contamination only caused a limited S isotope variation (∼1 ‰) during the formation of the Dongwanzi intrusion. Using S isotopic compositions of cumulus apatite in clinopyroxenite, the parental magma has δ34S values of ∼ + 7.9 ‰. Such high δ34S values are best explained by sub-arc mantle metasomatism rather than by crustal contamination. Collectively, our study highlights that S isotopic composition of apatite can be used to track the S isotope evolution and to constrain S sources in arc mafic-ultramafic cumulates.

title: Coupled δ 18 O–δ 13 C covariation and depositional architecture diagnose hydrologic state in barrage-cascade tufa systems
description: Publication date: 30 September 2026 Source: Chemical Geology, Volume 720 Author(s): Khalil Azennoud, Yassine Ait Brahim, Franziska Lechleitner, Hai Cheng, Radouan El Bamiki, Abdennasser Baali, Mohammed Hssaisoune, Hicham El Asmi, Xiaodong Jiang, Heather Stoll
abstract: Tufa carbonates are widely distributed terrestrial archives, yet lamina-scale geochemistry and system-scale depositional architecture have traditionally been studied in isolation: the former as a climate proxy, the latter as a geomorphic question. Here we show that these two scales are coupled, and that their coupling provides a direct diagnostic of hydrologic state in barrage-cascade systems. Combining U-Th chronology, petrography, stable isotope geochemistry, and geomorphic observations from a groundwater-fed barrage-cascade system in northern Morocco, we resolve six independent depositional intervals from the Middle Pleistocene to the Late Holocene, each preserving laminated microbialites and most retaining well-developed buttress architectures. Across these intervals, the magnitude of microbialite δ18Oc–δ13Cc covariation tracks upstream pool confinement and water residence time, defining a continuum from hydrologically open to evaporatively restricted configurations. These geochemical states correspond systematically to differences in buttress size, relief, and stacking geometry, providing an independent architectural validation of the proxy. This dual-scale approach helps reduce the ambiguity of single-proxy interpretations in continental carbonate archives. Comparison with modeled precipitation and regional context suggests that hydrologic state is better explained by temperature-modulated carbonate productivity and barrage-growth feedbacks than precipitation-driven discharge alone. These results establish a process-based framework that resolves barrage-cascade tufa systems as integrated geochemical–architectural archives of Earth-surface hydrology.

title: New evidence for normal seawater dolomitization in the middle Permian
description: Publication date: 30 September 2026 Source: Chemical Geology, Volume 720 Author(s): Heting Gao, Jiakai Hou, Manfei Chen, Xi Li, Sheng Li, Jianing Wang, Guangyou Zhu
abstract: Whether normal seawater drives platform-scale dolomitization remains debated. The viability of conventional evaporative brine or hydrothermal models is questioned by new studies favoring normal or slightly modified seawater.
